docs.title: Self-Assessment
docs.text:
Answer the following questions without looking back at the walkthroughs. If you get stuck, that topic is worth revisiting.

1. What smbclient flag provides the password inline with the username?

2. What does NT_STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE tell you, and what does it NOT tell you?

3. What is the difference between password spraying and brute forcing?

4. Why is CrackMapExec preferred over Hydra for modern SMB targets?

5. What does the --continue-on-success flag do in CrackMapExec?

6. Why should you enumerate usernames before attempting credential attacks?

7. List the seven phases of the complete SMB attack chain.

docs.title: Command Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
Keep the following reference handy throughout the rest of the workbook. These commands cover every technique from the chapter.

Command What It Does smbclient //<target>/share -U user%pass Authenticate to SMB share with inline credentials smbclient //<target>/IPC$ -U user%pass -c 'exit' Test credentials against IPC$ (credential validation) for pass in ...; do smbclient ...; done Bash loop for multi-password testing while read pass; do ...; done < passwords.txt Test passwords from a file crackmapexec smb <target> -u user -p wordlist.txt Brute force single user with CrackMapExec crackmapexec smb <target> -u users.txt -p wordlist.txt Brute force multiple users crackmapexec smb <target> -u user -p pass --shares List accessible shares after authentication crackmapexec smb <target> ... --continue-on-success Keep testing after finding valid credentials rpcclient -U "" -N <target> -c 'enumdomusers' \| grep -oP 'user:\[\K[^\]]+' > users.txt Extract usernames to a file

docs.title: Connect the Dots: What Comes Next
docs.text: You can now discover credentials for SMB; the Windows file-sharing protocol. But SMB is just one service on a Windows machine. Your Nmap scans from Chapter 1 also found RDP (port 3389). Chapter 4 applies the same reconnaissance and credential-testing methodology to Remote Desktop Protocol. The tools change; you will use xfreerdp instead of smbclient: but the workflow remains the same: discover the service, enumerate what you can, and test credentials to gain access.

docs.title: Self-Assessment Answer Key
docs.text:
1. The % separator: -U user%password passes the password inline. Example: smbclient //target/share -U admin%password.

2. It tells you the credentials are invalid. It does NOT tell you whether the username or the password (or both) are wrong; this is intentional to prevent username enumeration through the login process.

3. Password spraying tests one password against many users (safer, avoids lockout). Brute forcing tests many passwords against one user (faster for single targets, higher lockout risk).

4. Hydra's SMB module only supports SMBv1, which is disabled on modern systems. CrackMapExec supports SMBv2/v3 natively and provides additional post-authentication capabilities.

5. By default, CrackMapExec stops after finding the first valid credential pair. --continue-on-success keeps testing all remaining combinations, which is essential when multiple users may have weak passwords.

6. Enumeration eliminates guesswork. Testing known usernames with a password list is far more efficient than guessing both. It also ensures you do not miss accounts like service accounts (svc_*) that may have elevated privileges.

7. (1) Service discovery, (2) Share enumeration, (3) Anonymous access testing, (4) Null session enumeration, (5) Username extraction, (6) Credential attack, (7) Authenticated access and data retrieval.

docs.title: Why RDP Matters
docs.text:
Chapter 3 gave you authenticated access to SMB shares; you discovered credentials and downloaded files from protected directories. But file shares are only one service on a Windows machine. Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) provides something far more powerful: a full graphical desktop session on the target, as if you were sitting in front of the machine. An attacker with valid RDP credentials can browse files, run programs, install software, and access anything the logged-in user can reach. In a penetration test, gaining RDP access is often the turning point between "I found some data" and "I own this system."

Your Nmap scans from earlier chapters likely already revealed port 3389 on the FinanceCorp target. You noticed it, noted it, and moved on. Now you come back to that port with a plan.

docs.title: What Is RDP?
docs.text:
Remote Desktop Protocol is a proprietary protocol developed by Microsoft that allows a user to connect to another computer over a network and interact with its full graphical desktop. RDP listens on TCP port 3389 by default and is built into every version of Windows since XP. System administrators use it daily to manage servers without physical access. Attackers target it because a successful connection grants the same level of access as sitting at the keyboard.

The target in these exercises runs xrdp, an open-source RDP server commonly found on Linux systems configured to accept RDP connections. Nmap identifies xrdp as ms-wbt-server (Microsoft Windows-Based Terminal Server) because it speaks the same protocol as native Windows RDP. From the client side, connecting to xrdp feels identical to connecting to a Windows machine; the tools and techniques are the same.

RDP is one of the most commonly exposed services on the internet. Shodan regularly indexes hundreds of thousands of RDP endpoints, and credential-based attacks against RDP are a leading initial access vector for ransomware operators. Understanding how to detect, enumerate, and test RDP is essential for any penetration tester.

docs.title: How RDP Differs from SMB
docs.text:
SMB and RDP are both Windows-centric protocols, but they serve very different purposes. Recognizing the distinction helps you understand why gaining RDP access is a more significant finding than SMB access alone.

SMB (port 445) provides file and printer sharing. When you authenticate to an SMB share, you can list directories, read files, and write files; but only within the shares that the administrator has configured. You cannot run programs, install software, or interact with the system beyond file operations. SMB access is like having the key to a filing cabinet.

RDP (port 3389) provides a full interactive desktop session. When you authenticate over RDP, you see the target's desktop, taskbar, and applications. You can open a terminal and run any command the user account allows. You can browse the entire filesystem, not just specific shares. You can launch web browsers to access internal applications, open email clients, or connect to databases. RDP access is like sitting down at the computer itself.

In a penetration test report, SMB credential compromise is a significant finding. RDP credential compromise is a critical finding, because the scope of what an attacker can do with a desktop session far exceeds what they can do with file share access alone.

docs.title: The RDP Attack Workflow
docs.text:
The six labs in this chapter follow the same structured workflow that you used for SMB. Repeating the same methodology across different protocols reinforces the pattern and builds the habit of working systematically.

graph TD
    A["1. Service Detection<br/>Is RDP running?"]
    A --> B["2. Enumeration<br/>What can we learn?"]
    B --> C["3. Manual Access<br/>Do known creds work?"]
    C --> D["4. Credential Guessing<br/>Try common passwords"]
    D --> E["5. Brute Force<br/>Automate the attack"]
    E --> F["6. Post-Access<br/>What can we do?"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style F fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff

Each phase answers a specific question. Detection asks "is the service present?" Enumeration asks "what configuration details can we learn without credentials?" Manual access asks "do any known credentials work?" Credential guessing and brute force ask "can we discover unknown credentials?" Post-access asks "what is the real-world impact of this compromise?" By the time you finish all six labs, you will have answered every question in the chain.

docs.title: What Will You Learn?
docs.text:
The six labs in this chapter take you from discovering the RDP service to establishing a full graphical session and retrieving data from the target desktop. Each lab builds on the previous one, following the same methodology you used for SMB: discover, enumerate, test, exploit.

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Detect RDP services running on port 3389 using Nmap
  • Enumerate RDP version details, encryption levels, and NTLM information using NSE scripts
  • Connect to an RDP session using xfreerdp with known credentials
  • Test common credential combinations against RDP manually
  • Perform automated brute force attacks against RDP using Hydra
  • Navigate a full RDP desktop session and retrieve files through multiple methods

docs.title: Lab Progression
docs.text:
The six labs follow a deliberate path from passive detection to full interactive access. Each lab introduces one new capability.

graph LR

Exercise Title Key Commands 4.1 RDP Service Detection nmap -p 3389 -sV -Pn <target_ip> 4.2 RDP Version Enumeration nmap --script rdp-enum-encryption,rdp-ntlm-info <target_ip> 4.3 RDP Manual Connection Test xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:admin /p:password /cert:ignore 4.4 RDP Credential Guessing xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:admin /p:<guess> /cert:ignore 4.5 RDP Brute Force Attack hydra -l admin -P wordlist.txt rdp://<target_ip> 4.6 RDP Session Access and Flag Retrieval xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:admin /p:qwerty +clipboard /dynamic-resolution

Notice how the progression mirrors Chapter 3: detect the service, learn about its configuration, attempt manual access, guess credentials, automate the guessing, and then exploit successful credentials for full access.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
Make sure the following are in place before beginning Exercise 4.1:

  • You have completed Chapter 3 (SMB Credential Attacks)
  • You understand basic Nmap scanning from Chapter 1
  • Your VPN is connected and your terminal is open
  • You have a Kali Linux terminal with nmap, xfreerdp, and hydra installed (pre-installed on most Kali builds)
  • You have verified connectivity to the target by pinging it or running a quick Nmap scan
  • You are comfortable reading Nmap output (service names, version strings, script results)

If any of the earlier chapter concepts feel unclear, review those labs before proceeding. The techniques here assume you are comfortable with port scanning, service detection, and the general credential-attack workflow.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: In Chapter 3, you exploited SMB by testing credentials against file shares. Before you can attack any service, you need to confirm it exists and is reachable. RDP runs on a different port than SMB, and detecting it requires a targeted scan. Exercise 4.1 establishes the foundation for every lab that follows by confirming that RDP is running on the target.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
FinanceCorp has expanded the scope of your penetration test. James Mitchell wants you to assess all remote access services, not just file shares. Your earlier Nmap scans hinted at port 3389 being open, but you never investigated it. Now you need to confirm whether RDP is running, identify the service behind the port, and document your findings before moving to deeper enumeration.

The target provides an SSH account for flag retrieval: username rdpuser, password password123.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Scan port 3389 on the target to determine if RDP is running
  • Use Nmap service version detection to identify the RDP implementation
  • Understand the difference between port state and service identification
  • Capture the flag

docs.title: Background: RDP and Port 3389
docs.text:
Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) uses TCP port 3389 by default. When a system administrator enables remote desktop on a Windows server, the operating system begins listening on that port for incoming connections. Any client that speaks the RDP protocol can then negotiate a session.

Port 3389 is one of the most commonly scanned ports on the internet. Automated scanners and botnets continuously probe for open RDP endpoints because a successful connection grants full graphical access to the target system. Ransomware groups frequently purchase lists of compromised RDP credentials on dark web marketplaces, making RDP detection and hardening a critical part of any security assessment.

When Nmap detects an RDP service, it reports the service name as ms-wbt-server: short for "Microsoft Windows-Based Terminal Server." The target in these exercises runs xrdp, an open-source implementation, but Nmap still reports it as ms-wbt-server because xrdp speaks the same protocol. You cannot distinguish xrdp from native Windows RDP based on the service name alone; deeper enumeration (covered in Exercise 4.2) is needed for that.

graph LR
    A["Kali Linux<br/>Attacker"]
    B["windows-target<br/>Port 3389 (xrdp)"]
    A; "SYN to port 3389" --> B
    B; "SYN-ACK" --> A
    A; "Version probe" --> B
    B; "ms-wbt-server banner" --> A

docs.title: Tool Primer: Nmap for RDP Detection
docs.text:
You have used Nmap in Chapters 1 through 3. For RDP detection, three flags are essential.

Flag Purpose -p 3389 Scan only port 3389 (targeted, fast) -sV Probe the port to determine the service version -Pn Skip host discovery (assume the host is up)

Why use -Pn? Many firewalls block ICMP ping requests. Without -Pn, Nmap may decide the host is down and skip the scan entirely. Using -Pn forces Nmap to scan the port regardless of whether the host responds to pings.

Basic RDP detection command:

Detect RDP with a version scan

The three flags combine into the standard RDP detection scan: targeted port, version probe, and skipped host discovery.

nmap -p 3389 -sV -Pn <target_ip>

Sample output when RDP is open:

PORT     STATE SERVICE       VERSION
3389/tcp open  ms-wbt-server xrdp

Sample output when RDP is closed:

PORT     STATE  SERVICE
3389/tcp closed ms-wbt-server

The STATE column tells you whether the port is reachable. The SERVICE column tells you what protocol Nmap believes is running. The VERSION column (when available) tells you the specific software behind the service.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment.

  • Navigate to Exercises --> RDP Exploitation --> Level 1
  • Click Launch on "RDP Service Detection"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Run a Quick Port Check
docs.text:
Before running a full version scan, confirm that port 3389 is open with a simple connection scan.

Quick port check on 3389

A connection scan is faster because it does not probe for version information. Replace <target_ip> with the IP shown in the Active Lab View.

nmap -p 3389 -Pn <target_ip>

You should see port 3389 listed as open. If it shows as filtered or closed, wait 30 seconds for the lab environment to finish starting and scan again.

docs.title: Step 3: Run a Version Detection Scan
docs.text:
Now run the full version scan to identify the service and software behind port 3389.

Identify the RDP service version

The -sV flag probes the open port so Nmap can name the service and, where possible, the implementation.

nmap -p 3389 -sV -Pn <target_ip>

Examine the output carefully. You should see three key pieces of information in the results:

  • PORT: 3389/tcp
  • SERVICE: ms-wbt-server
  • VERSION: xrdp

The service name ms-wbt-server confirms that the port is running the RDP protocol. The version string xrdp tells you the specific implementation. Record both of these values; you will need them for your findings.

docs.title: Step 4: Run a Full Scan
docs.text:
To gather as much information as possible in a single scan, combine version detection with default scripts and OS detection.

Run a fuller scan with default scripts

The -sC flag runs Nmap's default script collection against the detected service.

nmap -p 3389 -sV -sC -Pn <target_ip>

For RDP, the default scripts may attempt to gather encryption information and certificate details. Compare the output from the previous step; you should see additional information in the script results section.

docs.title: Step 5: Retrieve the Flag via SSH
docs.text:
The flag for this exercise is stored in a file on the target system. After confirming that RDP is running, connect to the target using SSH to retrieve it.

Connect to the target over SSH

SSH gives you a shell on the target so you can read the flag file directly. Log in as rdpuser with the password password123 when prompted. The same rdpuser:password123 credentials are listed in the lab scenario.

ssh rdpuser@<target_ip>

Once connected, read the flag file.

Read the flag file on the target

The cat command runs in your SSH session on the target host and prints the flag stored in the user's home directory.

cat /home/rdpuser/flag.txt

The flag is in OCR{<flag_here>} format. Copy it before you disconnect.

Close the SSH session

The exit command leaves the target shell and returns you to your Kali prompt so you can paste the flag into the Submit Flag form.

exit

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Take a moment to think through these questions. They reinforce the concepts behind each step you performed.

1. Why does Nmap report the service as ms-wbt-server even though the target is running xrdp (a Linux application)?

Reveal Answer

Nmap identifies services by the protocol they speak, not by the operating system hosting them. xrdp implements the RDP protocol, which is the same protocol that Microsoft's Windows-Based Terminal Server uses. Nmap matches the protocol signature and assigns the standard service name. The VERSION field provides the more specific identification.

2. What is the risk of having RDP exposed on port 3389 without any additional protection?

Reveal Answer

An exposed RDP port is directly accessible to anyone on the network (or the internet, if publicly facing). Attackers can attempt credential guessing, brute force attacks, or exploit known RDP vulnerabilities like BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708). Without network-level restrictions such as VPN requirements, IP whitelisting, or Network Level Authentication (NLA), the service is open to automated attacks around the clock.

3. You used the -Pn flag to skip host discovery. In what situation would omitting -Pn cause you to miss an open port?

Reveal Answer

If the target's firewall blocks ICMP echo requests (pings), Nmap without -Pn will conclude the host is down and skip the port scan entirely. The port could be wide open, but you would never know because Nmap never sent a probe to it. Always use -Pn when scanning through firewalls or when you already know the target IP is correct.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• RDP runs on TCP port 3389 by default and provides full graphical remote access to the target
  • nmap -p 3389 -sV -Pn is the standard command for detecting and identifying an RDP service
  • Nmap reports RDP as ms-wbt-server regardless of whether the server is Windows-native or xrdp
  • The -Pn flag prevents Nmap from skipping hosts that do not respond to ping
  • Detecting the service is the first step; the next exercise digs deeper with NSE scripts to enumerate encryption levels, NTLM details, and protocol versions

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Exercise 4.1 confirmed that RDP is running on port 3389 and identified the service as xrdp. Knowing the service exists is useful, but a penetration tester needs more detail: what encryption levels are supported, what authentication information leaks through the protocol, and whether the server is vulnerable to known exploits. Nmap's NSE (Nmap Scripting Engine) scripts extract exactly that information.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
After confirming that FinanceCorp's target has RDP exposed, James Mitchell asks for a deeper assessment. He wants to know the encryption strength of the RDP service, whether the server leaks any domain or hostname information through NTLM negotiation, and whether the service might be vulnerable to BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708); a critical RDP vulnerability that allows remote code execution without authentication. You will use targeted NSE scripts to answer all three questions.

The target provides an SSH account for flag retrieval: username rdpuser, password password123.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Use NSE scripts to enumerate RDP encryption levels and security protocols
  • Extract NTLM authentication information (hostname, domain, OS version) from the RDP handshake
  • Examine SSL/TLS certificate details on the RDP service
  • Understand the BlueKeep vulnerability and its relevance to RDP assessments
  • Capture the flag

docs.title: Background: RDP Security Layers
docs.text:
RDP supports multiple security configurations, and the level of protection varies significantly between them. Understanding these layers helps you assess how well the target is defended.

RDP can operate in three security modes:

  • Standard RDP Security: the original encryption built into the RDP protocol. It uses RSA for key exchange and RC4 for bulk encryption. Known weaknesses in this mode allow man-in-the-middle attacks.
  • TLS (Transport Layer Security): wraps the RDP session in a standard TLS tunnel, the same encryption used by HTTPS. Significantly stronger than standard RDP security.
  • CredSSP (Credential Security Support Provider): adds Network Level Authentication (NLA), which requires the user to authenticate before the full RDP session is established. NLA is the strongest option because it prevents unauthenticated users from reaching the login screen.

A server that supports only Standard RDP Security without TLS or NLA is significantly weaker than one requiring CredSSP. Your enumeration will reveal which modes the target supports.

BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) is a critical vulnerability disclosed in May 2019 that affects the RDP service on older Windows systems (Windows 7, Windows Server 2008). It allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code by sending specially crafted requests to the RDP service. BlueKeep is "wormable"; meaning it can spread from machine to machine without user interaction. While the lab target (xrdp on Linux) is not vulnerable to BlueKeep, understanding the vulnerability is essential because you will encounter Windows RDP targets in real assessments.

graph TD
    A["RDP Security Modes"]
    A --> B["Standard RDP Security<br/>RC4 encryption, weak"]
    A --> C["TLS Security<br/>Same as HTTPS"]
    A --> D["CredSSP / NLA<br/>Pre-authentication required"]

    style B fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style C fill:#f0ad4e,color:#fff
    style D fill:#5cb85c,color:#fff

docs.title: Tool Primer: Nmap NSE Scripts for RDP
docs.text:
The Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE) extends Nmap's capabilities beyond port scanning. Three scripts are particularly relevant for RDP enumeration.

Script Purpose rdp-enum-encryption Lists supported encryption protocols and security layers rdp-ntlm-info Extracts NTLM authentication details (hostname, domain, OS) ssl-cert Retrieves the SSL/TLS certificate (if TLS is enabled)

Running multiple scripts at once:

Run three RDP NSE scripts in one scan

Comma-separating the script names tells Nmap to run all three against the same port in a single connection.

nmap -p 3389 -Pn --script rdp-enum-encryption,rdp-ntlm-info,ssl-cert <target_ip>

Sample rdp-enum-encryption output:

| rdp-enum-encryption:
|   Security layer
|     CredSSP (NLA): SUCCESS
|     CredSSP with Early User Auth: SUCCESS
|     Native RDP: SUCCESS
|     RDSTLS: SUCCESS
|     SSL: SUCCESS
|   RDP Encryption level: Client Compatible
|     40-bit RC4: SUCCESS
|     56-bit RC4: SUCCESS
|     128-bit RC4: SUCCESS
|     FIPS 140-1: SUCCESS
|_  RDP Protocol Version: Unknown

Sample rdp-ntlm-info output:

| rdp-ntlm-info:
|   Target_Name: FINANCECORP
|   NetBIOS_Domain_Name: FINANCECORP
|   NetBIOS_Computer_Name: WIN-DC01
|   DNS_Domain_Name: financecorp.local
|   DNS_Computer_Name: WIN-DC01.financecorp.local
|_  Product_Version: 10.0.17763

The NTLM information is especially valuable because it reveals internal hostnames, domain names, and sometimes the exact Windows version; all without requiring any authentication.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment.

  • Navigate to Exercises --> RDP Exploitation --> Level 2
  • Click Launch on "RDP Version Enumeration"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Run the RDP Encryption Enumeration Script
docs.text:
Start with the encryption enumeration script to discover what security modes the target supports.

Enumerate RDP encryption modes

The rdp-enum-encryption script lists every supported security layer and encryption strength. Replace <target_ip> with the IP shown in the Active Lab View.

nmap -p 3389 -Pn --script rdp-enum-encryption <target_ip>

Examine the output carefully. Look for which security layers returned SUCCESS and which encryption levels are supported. Pay attention to whether weak encryption (40-bit RC4) is accepted; a finding worth noting in any real assessment.

docs.title: Step 3: Run the NTLM Information Script
docs.text:
The NTLM info script extracts authentication metadata from the RDP handshake. No credentials are needed for this; the information leaks during the initial protocol negotiation.

Extract NTLM info from the RDP handshake

The rdp-ntlm-info script reads the hostname, domain, and OS version that the server leaks during protocol negotiation.

nmap -p 3389 -Pn --script rdp-ntlm-info <target_ip>

Record every field in the output. The Target_Name, NetBIOS_Computer_Name, and DNS_Domain_Name fields are reconnaissance gold. They reveal the internal naming structure of the organization without requiring any access.

docs.title: Step 4: Check the SSL Certificate
docs.text:
If the target supports TLS for RDP, the SSL certificate may contain additional information such as hostnames, organization names, and validity dates.

Retrieve the RDP SSL certificate

The ssl-cert script pulls the certificate when the service offers a TLS layer.

nmap -p 3389 -Pn --script ssl-cert <target_ip>

Look at the Subject and Issuer fields in the certificate. Self-signed certificates are common on internal servers and indicate that the organization has not deployed a proper PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) for RDP.

docs.title: Step 5: Run All Scripts Together
docs.text:
For efficiency, combine all three scripts into a single scan. Running them together saves time because Nmap only needs to establish one connection to the target.

Run all three scripts together

Comma-separating the three script names runs the full enumeration in one pass against the same connection.

nmap -p 3389 -Pn --script rdp-enum-encryption,rdp-ntlm-info,ssl-cert <target_ip>

Compare the combined output with the individual results from Steps 2-4. The information should be identical, but having it in one output makes documentation easier.

docs.title: Step 6: Understand BlueKeep Context
docs.text:
BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) targets a flaw in the RDP service on Windows 7, Windows Server 2008, and Windows Server 2008 R2. Nmap has a detection script for it.

Test for the MS12-020 RDP vulnerability

The rdp-vuln-ms12-020 script probes for a known RDP code-execution flaw that you would run against Windows targets.

nmap -p 3389 -Pn --script rdp-vuln-ms12-020 <target_ip>

The lab target runs xrdp on Linux, so it is not vulnerable to BlueKeep or MS12-020. However, in a real engagement, you would always run vulnerability-specific scripts against Windows RDP targets. A positive result for BlueKeep is a critical finding that should be reported immediately.

docs.title: Step 7: Retrieve the Flag via SSH
docs.text:
Connect to the target using SSH to retrieve the flag for this exercise.

Connect to the target over SSH

SSH gives you a shell on the target so you can read the flag file directly. Log in as rdpuser with the password password123 when prompted. The same rdpuser:password123 credentials are listed in the lab scenario.

ssh rdpuser@<target_ip>

Once connected, read the flag file.

Read the flag file on the target

The cat command runs in your SSH session on the target host and prints the flag stored in the user's home directory.

cat /home/rdpuser/flag.txt

The flag is in OCR{<flag_here>} format. Copy it before you disconnect.

Close the SSH session

The exit command leaves the target shell and returns you to your Kali prompt so you can paste the flag into the Submit Flag form.

exit

docs.text: Submit the flag you retrieved from /home/rdpuser/flag.txt in the OCR{<flag_here>} format to the platform.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Take a moment to think through these questions. They reinforce the concepts behind each step you performed.

1. The target supports 40-bit RC4 encryption for RDP. Why is accepting weak encryption a security concern, even if stronger options are also available?

Reveal Answer

An attacker who can perform a man-in-the-middle attack on the network could force the RDP session to downgrade to 40-bit encryption. 40-bit keys can be brute-forced in seconds on modern hardware. If the server only accepted 128-bit or FIPS 140-1 encryption, the downgrade attack would fail. Accepting weak encryption gives attackers options they should not have.

2. The rdp-ntlm-info script revealed the internal domain name and hostname without any authentication. Why is this a concern?

Reveal Answer

Internal naming conventions reveal organizational structure. A domain name like financecorp.local confirms the Active Directory domain. Hostnames like WIN-DC01 suggest a domain controller. An attacker can use this information to plan targeted attacks, craft phishing emails with believable internal references, or guess additional hostnames following the same naming pattern. Leaking internal infrastructure details to unauthenticated users violates the principle of least privilege.

3. The lab target runs xrdp on Linux and is not vulnerable to BlueKeep. How would you adjust your approach if the target were a Windows Server 2008 R2 machine?

Reveal Answer

You would immediately run the BlueKeep detection script (nmap --script rdp-vuln-ms12-020 or a dedicated BlueKeep scanner). If the system were vulnerable, you would flag it as a critical finding requiring immediate patching. BlueKeep allows unauthenticated remote code execution, making it far more severe than weak credentials. You would also check whether the system has been patched (KB4499175 for Server 2008 R2) and recommend enabling NLA as a mitigation even after patching.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• NSE scripts extend Nmap from a port scanner into a detailed enumeration tool
  • rdp-enum-encryption reveals which security layers and encryption strengths the server accepts; weak encryption is a reportable finding
  • rdp-ntlm-info extracts hostnames, domain names, and OS versions without authentication; valuable reconnaissance data
  • BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) is a critical RDP vulnerability affecting older Windows systems; always test for it on Windows targets
  • Enumeration builds the intelligence you need before attempting connections. The next exercise uses what you have learned here to make your first RDP connection.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Exercises 4.1 and 4.2 confirmed that RDP is running and revealed its encryption configuration and NTLM information. All of that was passive; you gathered data without attempting to log in. Now you cross the line from reconnaissance into active exploitation. You have a set of known credentials (admin:password), and you will use them to establish your first full RDP session.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: During the FinanceCorp assessment, another team member discovered the credentials admin:password through a different attack vector; perhaps a configuration file left in an accessible share, or a sticky note photographed during a physical assessment. James Mitchell asks you to verify whether these credentials grant RDP access to the target server. If they do, you need to document the access level and retrieve any sensitive data visible from the desktop session.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Connect to the target's RDP service using xfreerdp with known credentials
  • Navigate the XFCE desktop environment within the RDP session
  • Verify that the credentials provide a working graphical session
  • Locate and retrieve the flag from the remote desktop
  • Capture the flag

docs.title: Background: How RDP Sessions Work
docs.text:
When you connect to an RDP server with valid credentials, the server creates a full desktop session for your user account. You see the same desktop, applications, and files that the user would see if they were physically sitting at the machine. Every action you take; opening files, running commands, installing software; executes on the remote system, not on your local machine.

RDP sessions are not anonymous. The server logs every connection attempt, including the source IP address, the username, and the timestamp. In a real engagement, your RDP connections will appear in the Windows Event Log (or syslog on Linux/xrdp targets). The fact that connections are logged is something to note in your report; it means defenders can detect your activity if they are monitoring.

The target in these exercises runs the XFCE desktop environment through xrdp. XFCE is a lightweight Linux desktop that provides a taskbar, file manager, terminal emulator, and standard graphical applications. If you are familiar with Windows desktops, XFCE will feel similar; icons on the desktop, a taskbar at the bottom or top, and right-click context menus for common actions.

graph LR
    A["Kali Linux<br/>xfreerdp client"]
    B["windows-target<br/>xrdp server"]
    A; "RDP Protocol<br/>Port 3389" --> B
    B; "XFCE Desktop<br/>Session" --> C["Full graphical<br/>access"]

docs.title: Tool Primer: xfreerdp
docs.text:
xfreerdp is an open-source RDP client included with most Linux distributions. It connects to any RDP server; Windows-native or xrdp; and displays the remote desktop in a window on your local machine.

Basic xfreerdp connection syntax

The minimal command to open an RDP session supplies the target, a username, a password, and the certificate-ignore flag. Substitute the values for your engagement before running it.

xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:admin /p:password /cert:ignore

A successful run opens a remote desktop window. A failure returns the connection to the prompt with an error code.

Key flags explained:

Flag Purpose /v:<target_ip> Target server address (IP or hostname) /u:admin Username to authenticate with /p:password Password to authenticate with /cert:ignore Accept untrusted certificates without prompting /size:1280x720 Set the resolution of the remote desktop window +clipboard Enable clipboard sharing between local and remote systems

Why /cert:ignore? RDP servers typically use self-signed certificates. Without this flag, xfreerdp prompts you to manually accept the certificate every time you connect. In a lab environment, ignoring the certificate warning is safe and saves time.

What success looks like: A new window appears on your screen showing the remote desktop. You will see the XFCE desktop environment with a taskbar, desktop icons, and possibly a wallpaper.

What failure looks like: The terminal displays an error message such as ERRCONNECT_LOGON_FAILURE or ERRCONNECT_CONNECT_TRANSPORT_FAILED and no window appears. Authentication failures mean the credentials are wrong. Transport failures mean the service is unreachable.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment.

  • Navigate to Exercises --> RDP Exploitation --> Level 3
  • Click Launch on "RDP Manual Connection Test"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Verify RDP Is Accessible
docs.text:
Confirm RDP port is reachable

Before attempting a connection, confirm that port 3389 is reachable. The -Pn flag skips host discovery and treats the target as online, which avoids a false "host down" result when ICMP is filtered.

nmap -p 3389 -Pn <target_ip>

You should see port 3389 in the open state. If it shows as filtered, wait for the lab to finish initializing and try again.

docs.title: Step 3: Connect with xfreerdp
docs.text:
Open an RDP session with xfreerdp

Establish your first RDP session using the known credentials. The /cert:ignore flag accepts the self-signed certificate, and /size:1280x720 sets the window resolution.

xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:admin /p:password /cert:ignore /size:1280x720

A new window should appear within a few seconds, displaying the XFCE desktop. If you see an error instead of a desktop, check the following:

  • Is the target IP correct?
  • Is port 3389 confirmed open from Step 2?
  • Did you include /cert:ignore?

The graphical session an attacker gains the instant the credentials validate: the Applications menu, the panel showing the logged-in admin user, the Trash, File System, and Home desktop icons, and the launcher dock. The same desktop the user would see sitting at the physical machine is now under your control.

docs.title: Step 4: Explore the Desktop
docs.text:
Once the RDP session is established, take a moment to orient yourself in the remote desktop environment. The XFCE desktop has several key elements worth noting.

Look for the following:

  • Taskbar: usually at the top or bottom of the screen, with application launchers and a system tray
  • Desktop icons: files or shortcuts placed on the desktop surface
  • File Manager: accessible from the taskbar, shows the filesystem graphically
  • Terminal Emulator: accessible from the taskbar or by right-clicking the desktop, provides a command line

Open the file manager by clicking its icon in the taskbar or by right-clicking the desktop and selecting "Open Terminal Here" to get a command prompt.

A terminal opened inside the session lands you at the remote admin home prompt. Every command typed here runs on the victim host, not your Kali box, which is what makes interactive RDP access so much more powerful than file-share-only protocols.

docs.title: Step 5: Locate the Flag
docs.text:
The flag for this exercise is located at /home/admin/flag.txt. You can retrieve it using either the graphical file manager or the terminal. Both methods are valid; choose the one you are more comfortable with.

Method A; Using the Terminal:

Read the flag from the remote terminal

Open a terminal within the RDP session and run the following command on the target. The terminal runs inside the XFCE desktop, so the command executes on the remote machine.

cat /home/admin/flag.txt

The command prints the flag value in OCR{<flag_here>} format. Record it for submission.

Method B; Using the File Manager:

Open the file manager, navigate to /home/admin/, and double-click flag.txt to open it in a text editor.

The flag is in OCR{<flag_here>} format. Write it down or use clipboard sharing to copy it.

docs.title: Step 6: Enable Clipboard Sharing (if needed)
docs.text:
Reconnect with clipboard sharing enabled

If you did not include +clipboard in your initial connection, disconnect and reconnect with clipboard support enabled. The +clipboard flag turns on bidirectional copy and paste between your Kali machine and the remote desktop.

xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:admin /p:password \
  /cert:ignore /size:1280x720 +clipboard

With clipboard sharing active, you can copy text inside the RDP session (Ctrl+C) and paste it on your local machine (Ctrl+V). Copying the flag directly avoids transcription errors.

docs.title: Step 7: Disconnect the Session
docs.text: Close the RDP window by clicking the X button on the window frame, or press Ctrl+Alt+Enter to toggle fullscreen and then close. You can also disconnect from the terminal by killing the xfreerdp process.

Connection command used:

(paste the exact xfreerdp command you ran)

Desktop environment observed:

Element Present? (Yes/No) Taskbar Desktop icons File Manager Terminal Emulator

Flag retrieval method used: (Terminal / File Manager / Both)

Flag:

(paste the flag here)

docs.text: Submit the flag you retrieved from /home/admin/flag.txt in the OCR{<flag_here>} format to the platform.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Take a moment to think through these questions. They reinforce the concepts behind each step you performed.

1. The credentials admin:password gave you full desktop access. How does RDP access differ from SMB access in terms of what an attacker can do?

Reveal Answer

SMB access lets you read and write files on specific shares. RDP access gives you a full interactive desktop session; you can run programs, open browsers, access internal web applications, pivot to other systems, install backdoors, and interact with the system exactly as a legitimate user would. RDP access is significantly more dangerous than file share access because it provides complete control over the user's session.

2. You used /cert:ignore to bypass the certificate warning. In a real engagement, what should you do with the certificate information instead of ignoring it?

Reveal Answer

In a real engagement, you should examine the certificate details (issuer, subject, validity dates) and record them in your notes. A self-signed certificate is a finding worth reporting; it means the organization has not deployed proper certificate management for RDP. The certificate's subject name may also reveal internal hostnames or domain information useful for further reconnaissance.

3. The target runs XFCE, a Linux desktop environment. How would the experience differ if the target were a Windows Server?

Reveal Answer

On a Windows Server, you would see the standard Windows desktop with the Start menu, taskbar, and Windows Explorer. The file paths would use backslashes (C:\Users\admin\flag.txt instead of /home/admin/flag.txt). The command-line tools would be cmd.exe or PowerShell instead of bash. The underlying RDP protocol is identical; only the desktop environment and operating system differ. Your xfreerdp client works with both.

4. RDP connections are logged on the server. What log entries would your connection generate?

Reveal Answer

On a Linux/xrdp target, your connection generates entries in syslog and the xrdp log files (typically /var/log/xrdp.log and /var/log/xrdp-sesman.log). These logs record the source IP, username, connection time, and session duration. On a Windows target, RDP connections generate Event ID 4624 (successful logon) and Event ID 4625 (failed logon) in the Security Event Log. A security operations team monitoring these logs would see your activity.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• xfreerdp is the standard Linux RDP client for connecting to both Windows and xrdp targets
  • /cert:ignore bypasses certificate warnings; essential in lab environments, but examine certificates in real engagements
  • RDP provides full graphical desktop access, making it far more powerful than file-share-only protocols like SMB
  • The XFCE desktop on the target provides a file manager, terminal, and standard Linux tools through the graphical session
  • You connected with known credentials; but what if you do not have credentials? The next exercise explores manual credential guessing against RDP.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Exercise 4.3 gave you RDP access using credentials that were already known. In the real world, you rarely start with a valid username and password handed to you. Penetration testers often begin with nothing more than a service on an open port and a list of common guesses. Before reaching for automated tools, manual credential guessing helps you develop intuition about how authentication failures look, how long each attempt takes, and which credential patterns are worth trying first.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: James Mitchell has asked you to test whether any default or easily guessable credentials work on the FinanceCorp RDP service. You know the username admin exists on the system from your earlier enumeration. Your job is to systematically try common passwords, observe the results, and determine whether the account uses a weak password. The credentials from Exercise 4.3 (admin:password) have been changed; you need to discover the new password.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Manually test common credential combinations against the RDP service
  • Observe and interpret xfreerdp authentication error messages
  • Apply a structured approach to manual credential guessing
  • Discover valid credentials and establish an RDP session
  • Capture the flag

docs.title: Background: Manual Credential Guessing Strategy
docs.text:
Automated brute force tools test thousands of passwords per minute, but running them blindly wastes time and generates noise. A skilled tester starts with manual guessing; a small number of high-probability passwords chosen based on context. Manual guessing is quiet (fewer log entries), fast (you test the most likely candidates first), and educational (you learn how the service responds to failures).

Effective manual guessing follows a structured order, starting with the most commonly successful categories.

Category 1; Default credentials. Every service has well-known defaults. For RDP on a system with an admin account, the usual suspects are admin, password, admin123, and blank passwords.

Category 2; Keyboard patterns. Passwords like qwerty, 123456, abc123, and 1q2w3e4r appear in nearly every breach database. Users choose them because they are fast to type, not because they are secure.

Category 3; Organizational context. Knowing the company name is "FinanceCorp" lets you try patterns like FinanceCorp2024, Finance123, and Welcome1. These organizational passwords are especially common as initial passwords set by IT departments.

Category 4; Seasonal and date-based. Passwords like Summer2025, Winter2024, and January2025 are common in environments that force periodic password changes, because users pick the easiest pattern that meets complexity requirements.

A well-organized tester works through these categories in order, spending two to three minutes on manual guessing before escalating to automated tools. If the password falls in the first 10-15 guesses, you have saved significant time compared to launching a full brute force.

graph TD
    A["Start: Known username 'admin'"]
    A --> B["Try default creds<br/>admin, password, admin123"]
    B --> C["Try keyboard patterns<br/>qwerty, 123456, abc123"]
    C --> D["Try org-specific<br/>FinanceCorp2024, Finance123"]
    D --> E["Try seasonal<br/>Summer2025, Welcome1"]
    E --> F["Escalate to<br/>automated brute force"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style F fill:#d9534f,color:#fff

docs.title: Tool Primer: xfreerdp for Credential Testing
docs.text:
You already know xfreerdp from Exercise 4.3. For credential testing, the key behavior to understand is how xfreerdp reports authentication failures.

Test a single credential pair

To test one password, pass it with /p: and watch the result. Replace testpassword with the candidate you want to try.

xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:admin /p:testpassword /cert:ignore

A desktop window means the credentials are valid. An error returned to the prompt means they were rejected.

Successful authentication: A desktop window appears. The credentials are valid.

Failed authentication: The terminal displays an error and no window appears. The exact error message varies by configuration, but common failures look like the following output.

[ERROR][com.freerdp.core.connection] - ERRCONNECT_LOGON_FAILURE [0x00020014]

The error code 0x00020014 maps to ERRCONNECT_LOGON_FAILURE, which means the username or password was rejected. Just like SMB's NT_STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE, RDP does not tell you whether the username or the password was wrong; both produce the same error.

Testing quickly: Each failed xfreerdp attempt takes 2-5 seconds because the client must complete the full TLS handshake and authentication exchange before receiving the rejection. Plan accordingly; 10 manual guesses will take about 30-50 seconds.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment.

  • Navigate to Exercises --> RDP Exploitation --> Level 4
  • Click Launch on "RDP Credential Guessing"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Verify RDP Is Accessible
docs.text:
Confirm RDP port is reachable

Confirm that port 3389 is reachable on the target. The -Pn flag skips host discovery so a filtered ICMP response does not hide a live host.

nmap -p 3389 -Pn <target_ip>

Port 3389 should be in the open state before you proceed.

docs.title: Step 3: Test Default Credentials
docs.text:
Try default passwords one at a time

Start with the most commonly used default passwords. Try each one individually and observe the result. The first attempt tests the username-matches-password pattern.

xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:admin /p:admin /cert:ignore

If you see the LOGON_FAILURE error, the password admin is incorrect. Move to the next guess.

xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:admin /p:password /cert:ignore

Try the default from the previous exercise. If the password has been changed, you will see another failure.

xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:admin /p:admin123 /cert:ignore

Pay close attention to the response for each attempt. When you try admin123, the behavior should differ from the previous failures; instead of an error message, a desktop window should appear.

docs.title: Step 4: Confirm the Successful Connection
docs.text:
If the admin:admin123 attempt opens a desktop window, you have found valid credentials. The XFCE desktop should appear, confirming that the admin account uses the password admin123.

Take a moment to verify you have full access by opening the file manager or a terminal within the RDP session.

Confirmation that the guess landed: the XFCE desktop loads and a terminal opened inside the session sits at the remote admin prompt. The moment a failure error turns into a live desktop is the signal that the password is correct.

docs.title: Step 5: Record the Attempts
docs.text:
Documenting every attempt, not just the successful one, is essential for a penetration test report. A complete record shows the client that you followed a methodical approach.

Keep track of each credential pair you tested and its result using the table in the Record Your Findings section below.

docs.title: Step 6: Retrieve the Flag
docs.text:
Read the flag from the remote terminal

The flag is located at /home/admin/flag.txt. Open a terminal within the RDP session and read the file on the target. The terminal runs inside the remote desktop, so the command executes on the victim host.

cat /home/admin/flag.txt

The flag is in OCR{<flag_here>} format. Copy it using clipboard sharing or write it down.

docs.title: Step 7: Disconnect
docs.text: Close the RDP session by closing the desktop window or pressing Ctrl+Alt+Enter and then closing the window. You can also terminate xfreerdp from your local terminal with Ctrl+C.

docs.title: Record Your Findings
docs.text:
Credential testing log:

Successful credentials:

Username Password

Flag:

(paste the flag here)

docs.title: Step 8: Record the Flag
docs.text: Submit the flag you retrieved from /home/admin/flag.txt in the OCR{<flag_here>} format to the platform.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Take a moment to think through these questions. They reinforce the concepts behind each step you performed.

1. You found the password admin123 on your third attempt. In a real environment with account lockout after 5 failed attempts, would your approach still work?

Reveal Answer

Yes; three attempts is well within a typical lockout threshold of 5. Manual guessing with a short list of high-probability passwords is specifically designed to stay under lockout thresholds. An automated brute force testing hundreds of passwords would trigger lockout quickly, but targeted manual guessing is safe when you limit yourself to fewer than the lockout threshold minus one (to leave a margin of safety).

2. The password admin123 combines the username with a simple numeric suffix. What does this pattern reveal about how the password was likely created?

Reveal Answer

The password was probably set by an IT administrator as an initial or default password, using a predictable pattern of "username + numbers." Many organizations use this pattern for new accounts, expecting users to change the password on first login. If no password change is enforced, the initial password remains active indefinitely. Penetration testers should always try "username + common suffixes" (123, 1, 01, 2024) as one of their first guessing strategies.

3. Why is manual credential guessing preferred over automated brute force as a first step?

Reveal Answer

Manual guessing is quieter (fewer failed login attempts appear in logs), faster for high-probability passwords (you skip the thousands of unlikely passwords in a wordlist), and less likely to trigger account lockout or intrusion detection systems. It also gives you firsthand experience with the service's authentication behavior; how long each attempt takes, what error messages look like, and whether the service throttles connections. Starting manual and escalating to automated tools is the standard penetration testing methodology.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Manual credential guessing should always precede automated brute force attacks
  • Test passwords in priority order: default credentials, keyboard patterns, organizational context, seasonal patterns
  • The password admin123 follows the common "username + numbers" pattern; always include these in your first guesses
  • xfreerdp reports ERRCONNECT_LOGON_FAILURE for both wrong usernames and wrong passwords, preventing username enumeration through error messages
  • Manual guessing stays under account lockout thresholds, making it safer than automated tools in environments with lockout policies
  • You found the password in three tries. The next exercise automates the process for situations where manual guessing does not succeed quickly.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text: Exercise 4.4 demonstrated that manual guessing works when the password is among the first few candidates. But what happens when the password is not in your top 10 guesses? You need automation. In Chapter 3, you used CrackMapExec for SMB brute force because Hydra did not support SMBv2. For RDP, the situation is different; Hydra fully supports the RDP protocol and is the standard tool for automated RDP credential attacks.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: FinanceCorp has reset the admin password after your earlier findings. James Mitchell wants you to demonstrate that automated tools can still discover the new password if it remains weak. Your manual guesses from Exercise 4.4 no longer work, so you need to scale up. You will create a targeted wordlist and use Hydra to test every password in the list against the RDP service. The password policy at FinanceCorp still does not enforce complexity requirements; a fact you documented in earlier chapters.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Create a targeted wordlist containing common and contextual passwords
  • Use Hydra to perform an automated brute force attack against the RDP service
  • Interpret Hydra's output to identify valid credentials
  • Verify the discovered credentials by establishing an RDP session
  • Capture the flag

docs.title: Background: Automated Brute Force with Hydra
docs.text:
Hydra is a parallelized network login cracker that supports over 50 protocols, including RDP. It reads usernames and passwords from files or the command line, then tests every combination against the target service. Hydra handles connection management, retry logic, and result parsing automatically; the things that make manual testing tedious at scale.

How Hydra tests RDP credentials:

For each username-password combination, Hydra opens a connection to port 3389, performs the RDP authentication handshake, and checks whether the server accepted or rejected the credentials. Failed attempts produce a rejection message. Successful attempts produce an acceptance. Hydra reports the result for each attempt and, by default, stops after finding the first valid pair.

Wordlist strategy matters more than wordlist size. A focused list of 50 passwords built from breach data, keyboard patterns, and organizational context will often succeed faster than testing all 14 million entries in rockyou.txt. For a targeted assessment against FinanceCorp, your wordlist should include:

  • Default passwords: admin, password, admin123, changeme
  • Keyboard patterns: qwerty, 123456, abc123, 1q2w3e4r
  • Company patterns: FinanceCorp, Finance123, FinanceCorp2024
  • Seasonal patterns: Summer2025, Winter2024, Welcome1
  • Common weak passwords: letmein, monkey, dragon, master

Thread count and RDP: RDP authentication is slower than protocols like SSH or FTP because the TLS handshake adds overhead. Running too many parallel threads (connections) can overwhelm the target or trigger rate limiting. A conservative thread count of 4 is recommended for RDP brute force.

graph LR
    A["Wordlist<br/>(passwords.txt)"] --> B["Hydra<br/>RDP module"]
    B; "Thread 1" --> C["Target<br/>Port 3389"]
    B; "Thread 2" --> C
    B; "Thread 3" --> C
    B; "Thread 4" --> C
    C; "Success/Failure" --> B
    B --> D["Results<br/>Valid credentials"]

docs.title: Tool Primer: Hydra
docs.text:
Hydra is a command-line brute force tool. The basic syntax for an RDP attack specifies the username, password source, protocol, and target.

Basic Hydra RDP syntax

The minimal Hydra command for RDP takes a single username with -l, a password file with -P, and the rdp:// target. Substitute your wordlist filename and target IP before running it.

hydra -l admin -P wordlist.txt rdp://<target_ip>

Hydra prints a success line containing [3389][rdp] when it finds a valid pair.

Key flags:

Flag Purpose -l admin Single username to test (lowercase L) -L users.txt File containing multiple usernames (uppercase L) -p password Single password to test (lowercase p) -P wordlist.txt File containing multiple passwords (uppercase P) -t 4 Number of parallel threads (connections) -V Verbose mode; show every attempt as it happens -f Stop after finding the first valid credential pair rdp:// Protocol and target specification

Reading Hydra output:

Hydra prefixes each result with a status indicator. Failed attempts appear only in verbose mode (-V). Successful credentials are always displayed, regardless of verbosity.

[DATA] attacking rdp://10.0.0.5:3389/
[3389][rdp] host: 10.0.0.5   login: admin   password: qwerty
1 of 1 target successfully completed, 1 valid password found

The line containing [3389][rdp] followed by login: and password: is the success indicator. The username and password on that line are your valid credentials.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment.

  • Navigate to Exercises --> RDP Exploitation --> Level 5
  • Click Launch on "RDP Brute Force Attack"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Verify RDP Is Accessible
docs.text:
Confirm RDP port is reachable

Confirm that port 3389 is open before running the brute force attack. The -Pn flag skips host discovery so the scan does not give up when ICMP is filtered.

nmap -p 3389 -Pn <target_ip>

Port 3389 should be in the open state.

docs.title: Step 3: Create a Targeted Wordlist
docs.text:
Build a targeted wordlist

Build a wordlist that covers the most likely password categories. Create the file on your Kali machine. The heredoc writes each password on its own line into passwords.txt.

cat > passwords.txt << 'EOF'
password
admin
admin123
qwerty
123456
Password123
password123
letmein
welcome
changeme
abc123
monkey
dragon
master
1q2w3e4r
FinanceCorp
Finance123
FinanceCorp2024
Summer2025
Winter2024
Welcome1
iloveyou
trustno1
EOF

The wordlist contains 22 passwords. At approximately 3-5 seconds per attempt with 4 threads, Hydra should test the entire list in under 30 seconds. Verify the wordlist was created correctly by checking its line count.

wc -l passwords.txt

You should see 22 passwords.txt in the output.

docs.title: Step 4: Run Hydra in Verbose Mode
docs.text:
Run the Hydra brute force

Launch the brute force attack with verbose output so you can observe each attempt in real time. The -t 4 flag uses four threads, -V prints each attempt, and -f stops at the first success.

hydra -l admin -P passwords.txt -t 4 -V -f rdp://<target_ip>

Replace <target_ip> with the IP from the Active Lab View. Watch the output carefully as Hydra tests each password. You will see lines showing each attempt, and eventually a success line identifying the valid credentials.

The -f flag tells Hydra to stop immediately after finding the first valid password. Without it, Hydra would continue testing every remaining password in the list; wasteful when you only need one valid pair.

docs.title: Step 5: Identify the Valid Credentials
docs.text:
Look for the success line in the output. It should look similar to the following.

[3389][rdp] host: <target_ip>   login: admin   password: qwerty

The password qwerty is a keyboard pattern; the first six letters on the top row of a standard keyboard. It consistently ranks among the top 10 most commonly used passwords worldwide.

Hydra's RDP module reports false positives against xrdp

Hydra's rdp module is known to mis-report successes against xrdp. The xrdp service can return a response that Hydra reads as an acceptance even when the password is wrong, so the tool may print a bogus hit such as login: admin password: password. Never trust a Hydra RDP result on its own. Every reported pair must be confirmed with a real login (Step 6) before you record it as valid. If you see more than one reported password, the correct one is whichever actually opens a session. For these labs, the working credential is admin:qwerty.

docs.title: Step 6: Verify the Credentials
docs.text:
Treat Step 6 as mandatory, not optional. A Hydra RDP hit is only a candidate until a real client logs in with it.

Verify the discovered credentials

Confirm that each credential Hydra reported actually works by connecting with xfreerdp. Use the password from the Hydra success line. A genuine hit opens a desktop window; a false positive fails with ERRCONNECT_LOGON_FAILURE.

xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:admin /p:qwerty /cert:ignore /size:1280x720

A desktop window should appear, confirming that admin:qwerty is valid and provides RDP access. If a different password Hydra reported fails here, discard it as a false positive and try the next reported pair.

docs.title: Step 7: Retrieve the Flag
docs.text:
Read the flag from the remote terminal

Open a terminal within the RDP session and read the flag file on the target. The terminal runs inside the remote desktop, so the command executes on the victim host.

cat /home/admin/flag.txt

The flag is in OCR{<flag_here>} format. Copy it and disconnect from the RDP session.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Take a moment to think through these questions. They reinforce the concepts behind each step you performed.

1. You used 4 threads (-t 4) for the RDP brute force. What would happen if you increased the thread count to 64?

Reveal Answer

High thread counts can overwhelm the RDP service, causing connection timeouts, dropped connections, or service crashes. RDP authentication involves a full TLS handshake for each attempt, which is more resource-intensive than simpler protocols. Many RDP servers also implement connection rate limiting that throttles or blocks IPs making too many simultaneous connections. A conservative thread count (4-8) is more reliable and less likely to trigger defensive mechanisms or denial-of-service conditions.

2. The -f flag stopped Hydra after finding one valid password. When would you want to continue testing after a success?

Reveal Answer

If you suspect multiple user accounts might have weak passwords, you would omit -f so Hydra tests all combinations. In a real assessment with a user list file (-L users.txt), continuing after one success ensures you find every compromised account, not just the first one. Multiple valid credentials are important for the report because each one represents a separate finding, and different accounts may have different privilege levels.

3. In Chapter 3, you used CrackMapExec instead of Hydra for SMB because Hydra only supports SMBv1. Why does Hydra work for RDP but not for modern SMB?

Reveal Answer

Hydra's RDP module implements the standard RDP/TLS authentication protocol, which has not changed in the same way that SMB versioning has. SMB went through a fundamental protocol redesign from v1 to v2/v3, and Hydra's SMB module was never updated to support the new protocol. RDP's authentication mechanism remained consistent across versions, so Hydra's RDP module continues to work against both old and new RDP implementations. The takeaway is that tool compatibility depends on the specific protocol, not the tool itself; always verify your tool supports the target's protocol version.

4. Your wordlist had 22 entries and the password was found quickly. What would you do if none of these passwords worked?

Reveal Answer

You would escalate to larger wordlists. The rockyou.txt file (included with Kali Linux at /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt) contains over 14 million passwords from a real data breach. You could also generate custom wordlists using tools like cewl (which scrapes words from the organization's website) or crunch (which generates passwords from specific patterns). Before testing a massive list, you would also check for account lockout policies; testing 14 million passwords against an account that locks after 5 failures is counterproductive.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Hydra is the standard tool for automated RDP brute force attacks and fully supports the RDP protocol
  • Use -t 4 threads for RDP to avoid overwhelming the service; RDP authentication is slower than simpler protocols
  • The -f flag stops Hydra after the first valid credential pair, saving time when you only need one working login
  • Wordlist quality determines success; a targeted list of 20-50 passwords often outperforms a generic list of thousands
  • The password qwerty is a keyboard pattern found in nearly every breach database; always include keyboard patterns in your wordlists
  • You now have automated credential discovery for RDP. The next exercise uses your discovered credentials to establish a full session and explore the target's desktop environment in depth.

docs.title: Exercise 4.6: RDP Session Access and Flag Retrieval
Before You Begin
docs.text: Exercises 4.1 through 4.5 followed a clear progression: detect the service, enumerate its configuration, connect with known credentials, guess credentials manually, and brute force credentials automatically. Each lab built one skill. Now you combine everything into a complete RDP exploitation scenario; connecting with discovered credentials, navigating the desktop environment, and retrieving data through multiple methods. A penetration tester who can only find credentials but cannot operate within the session is only half effective.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
James Mitchell wants a complete demonstration of the RDP risk at FinanceCorp. Finding credentials is only part of the story; the client needs to see what an attacker can actually do once they are inside. You will establish a full RDP session with advanced options, navigate the target's desktop, and retrieve a flag file stored on the user's Desktop using three different methods. Your report should show that an attacker with RDP access has the same level of control as someone sitting at the physical machine.

Use the working credentials for this lab: username admin, password password123. The flag is on the admin Desktop at /home/admin/Desktop/flag.txt.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Connect to the target using xfreerdp with advanced session options (clipboard, drive sharing, dynamic resolution)
  • Navigate the remote XFCE desktop to locate files visually
  • Retrieve the flag using three different methods: terminal, file manager, and drive sharing
  • Demonstrate the full impact of RDP access in a penetration test context
  • Capture the flag

docs.title: Background: Post-Authentication RDP Capabilities
docs.text:
Gaining RDP access means more than just seeing a desktop. A full RDP session provides capabilities that make it one of the most valuable footholds in a penetration test.

Clipboard sharing allows you to copy and paste text between your local machine and the remote desktop. Passwords, file contents, and command output can be transferred instantly. In an attack scenario, an adversary could copy sensitive data from the target and paste it into their own notes without leaving any file transfer artifacts.

Drive redirection maps a local directory from your machine into the remote desktop's file system. The remote system sees your local folder as a network drive, allowing you to drag and drop files between systems. For a penetration tester, drive redirection means you can exfiltrate files from the target by simply copying them to the shared drive; no need for separate file transfer tools.

Dynamic resolution adjusts the remote desktop resolution to match your local window size. Resizing the window automatically changes the remote display, making it easier to work in the session without scrolling or squinting at a tiny viewport.

These features are all controlled by xfreerdp command-line flags. Each one adds a capability that mirrors what a real attacker would use after compromising RDP credentials.

graph TD
    A["xfreerdp Connection"]
    A --> B["Clipboard Sharing<br/>Copy/paste between systems"]
    A --> C["Drive Redirection<br/>Map local folder to remote"]
    A --> D["Dynamic Resolution<br/>Auto-resize display"]
    A --> E["Full Desktop Access<br/>Terminal, File Manager, Apps"]

    style A fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff

docs.title: Tool Primer: xfreerdp Advanced Options
docs.text:
Building on Exercise 4.3's basic connection, the following flags enable advanced session features.

Flag Purpose +clipboard Enable bidirectional clipboard sharing /drive:share,/tmp/rdp_share Map a local directory to a remote drive /dynamic-resolution Allow resolution changes when resizing the window /cert:ignore Accept untrusted certificates without prompting /size:1280x720 Set initial window resolution

Full xfreerdp connection with advanced options

The following command combines clipboard sharing, drive redirection, and dynamic resolution in one connection. Each flag adds a capability that mirrors what a real attacker would use after compromising RDP credentials.

xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:admin /p:password123 \
  /cert:ignore +clipboard \
  /drive:share,/tmp/rdp_share \
  /dynamic-resolution

A remote desktop window opens with all three features active.

Drive redirection explained: The /drive:share,/tmp/rdp_share flag tells xfreerdp to create a directory at /tmp/rdp_share on your local machine (if it does not already exist) and present it as a network drive named "share" inside the remote desktop. Any file you copy to that drive in the remote session will appear in /tmp/rdp_share on your local machine.

Create the local share directory

Before connecting with drive redirection, create the local share directory first. The -p flag makes the operation succeed even if the directory already exists.

mkdir -p /tmp/rdp_share

The command produces no output on success.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise
docs.text:
Open the platform in your browser and start the exercise environment.

  • Navigate to Exercises --> RDP Exploitation --> Level 6
  • Click Launch on "RDP Session Access and Flag Retrieval"
  • Wait for the status to change to Running
  • Note the target IP displayed in the Active Lab View

docs.title: Step 2: Prepare the Local Share Directory
docs.text:
Create and verify the local share directory

Create the directory that will be mapped into the remote session for file transfer.

mkdir -p /tmp/rdp_share

Verify the directory exists.

ls -ld /tmp/rdp_share

You should see the directory listed with appropriate permissions.

docs.title: Step 3: Connect with Advanced Options
docs.text:
Connect with all advanced features

Establish the RDP session with all advanced features enabled. The same combined flag set from the Tool Primer turns on clipboard, drive sharing, and dynamic resolution.

xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:admin /p:password123 \
  /cert:ignore +clipboard \
  /drive:share,/tmp/rdp_share \
  /dynamic-resolution

The XFCE desktop should appear in a new window. Try resizing the window; the remote desktop should adjust its resolution automatically thanks to the /dynamic-resolution flag.

docs.title: Step 4: Locate the Flag Visually
docs.text:
The flag for this exercise is on the user's Desktop at /home/admin/Desktop/flag.txt. Start by looking at the desktop surface itself.

Look for a file icon labeled flag.txt on the desktop. In the XFCE environment, desktop files appear as icons on the desktop surface. If the file is visible, you can double-click it to open it in the default text editor and read its contents.

If the file is not visible as a desktop icon, open the file manager from the taskbar and navigate to /home/admin/Desktop/.

docs.title: Step 5: Retrieve the Flag Using the Terminal (Method 1)
docs.text:
Open a terminal emulator within the RDP session. You can find it in the taskbar, or right-click the desktop and look for a "Terminal" or "Open Terminal Here" option.

Read the flag from the remote terminal

Once the terminal is open, read the flag file on the target. The terminal runs inside the remote desktop, so the command executes on the victim host.

cat /home/admin/Desktop/flag.txt

The flag is in OCR{<flag_here>} format. With clipboard sharing enabled, you can select the flag text in the remote terminal, copy it (Ctrl+Shift+C in most terminal emulators), and paste it directly on your local machine.

docs.title: Step 6: Retrieve the Flag Using the File Manager (Method 2)
docs.text:
Open the XFCE file manager (Thunar) from the taskbar. Navigate through the directory tree on the left panel.

Click through the following path: Home --> Desktop.

You should see flag.txt in the file listing. Double-click the file to open it in the text editor and read the flag contents. Having multiple retrieval methods available is important because some remote systems may have restricted terminal access or disabled certain GUI applications.

The Thunar file manager navigated to /home/admin/Desktop reveals the flag.txt file directly in the listing, no command line required. A file manager turns the RDP foothold into point-and-click data discovery, which is exactly how an attacker would sweep a compromised desktop for sensitive material.

docs.title: Step 7: Retrieve the Flag Using Drive Sharing (Method 3)
docs.text:
Drive sharing allows you to copy files from the remote system to your local machine through the mapped drive.

Copy the flag onto the mapped drive

Inside the RDP session, open a terminal and copy the flag to the shared drive. The command runs on the target and writes into the redirected drive path.

cp /home/admin/Desktop/flag.txt /media/cdrom/share/

The path /media/cdrom/share/ (or similar, depending on the xrdp configuration) is where the redirected drive appears in the remote filesystem. If that path does not exist, look for the mapped drive in the file manager under "Devices" or "Network" in the left panel.

Read the transferred flag on your local machine

After copying the file, check your local machine. The file should appear in your local share directory.

cat /tmp/rdp_share/flag.txt

If the drive mapping path differs on your system, you can also use the file manager within the RDP session to locate the mapped drive and drag the flag file to it.

docs.title: Step 8: Disconnect and Verify
docs.text:
Verify the transfer after disconnecting

Close the RDP session. Back on your local machine, verify that the flag was successfully transferred through drive sharing.

ls /tmp/rdp_share/
cat /tmp/rdp_share/flag.txt

You should see flag.txt in the directory and its contents should match what you saw in the remote terminal.
