Each lab demonstrated a different post-exploitation technique, but they share a common thread: once an attacker has shell access, the boundary between "limited user" and "full compromise" is often thinner than administrators realize.

docs.title: Self-Assessment
docs.text:
Answer these questions without looking at the answer key below. If you can answer all eight confidently, you have internalized the core skills of this chapter.

1. What six commands form the core of initial system enumeration after SSH access?

2. Why are environment variables a security risk, and how do you view them from a shell?

3. Name three types of history files an attacker should check beyond .bash_history.

4. What grep command extracts all IP addresses from a Bash history file?

5. What is the first command you should run to check for privilege escalation opportunities via sudo?

6. Why is (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/cat effectively equivalent to full root access?

7. What three files should an attacker prioritize reading after gaining sudo cat access?

8. How does a stolen root SSH private key enable lateral movement across an organization?

docs.title: Command Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
The table below collects every key command from this chapter into a single reference.

Command Purpose Exercise ssh user@<target_ip> Authenticate to the target via SSH All uname -a Display kernel version and architecture L3.1 hostname Print the system hostname L3.1 ip addr Show network interfaces and IP addresses L3.1 ps aux List all running processes L3.1 ss -tlnp Show listening TCP ports with process info L3.1 env Print all environment variables L3.1 /usr/local/bin/system-check Execute the custom admin script L3.1 cat ~/.bash_history Read Bash command history L3.2 cat ~/.mysql_history Read MySQL client history L3.2 cat ~/.python_history Read Python REPL history L3.2 grep -in "pass" ~/.bash_history Search history for passwords L3.2 grep -in "key\|token" ~/.bash_history Search history for API keys and tokens L3.2 grep -oE "[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+" ~/.bash_history Extract all IP addresses from history L3.2 sudo -l List sudo permissions for current user L3.3 sudo cat /root/flag.txt Read a root-owned file via sudo L3.3 sudo cat /etc/shadow Extract password hashes L3.3 sudo cat /root/.ssh/id_rsa Read the root SSH private key L3.3 sudo ls -la /root/ List root home directory contents L3.3

docs.title: Connect the Dots: What Comes Next
docs.text:
Chapter L3 completes the Linux post-exploitation track. Across Chapters L1 through L3, you progressed from service enumeration to SSH authentication to full post-exploitation and privilege escalation. You can now scan a Linux target, gain authenticated access, gather intelligence, and escalate to root; the complete attack lifecycle on a Linux host.

These Linux skills do not exist in isolation. In real penetration test engagements, Linux and Windows systems coexist on the same network. The credentials you harvest from Linux history files may unlock Windows services. The network topology you map from a Linux pivot point may reveal Windows domain controllers. The password hashes you extract from /etc/shadow may match passwords reused on Windows accounts.

The Windows track (Chapters 4-7) covers RDP exploitation, WinRM command execution, MSSQL database attacks, and LDAP enumeration. Consider how the post-exploitation methodology you practiced here; enumerate, harvest, escalate; applies identically to Windows targets, just with different commands and different tools. A penetration tester who can operate across both Linux and Windows environments delivers a thorough assessment that reflects how real attackers move through hybrid networks.

Review your notes from all three chapters. Verify that you can explain the purpose of every command, describe the attack chain from scan to root, and articulate why each finding matters to FinanceCorp's security posture.

docs.title: Self-Assessment Answer Key
docs.text:
1. The six core enumeration commands are uname -a (OS and kernel), hostname (machine identity), ip addr (network position), ps aux (running processes), ss -tlnp (listening ports), and env (environment variables). Together, they provide complete situational awareness of the compromised host.

2. Environment variables are readable by any process in the user's shell session. Developers frequently store database passwords, API keys, and connection strings as environment variables. Running env displays all of them in plaintext. Any attacker with shell access can read these values immediately.

3. Beyond .bash_history, attackers should check .mysql_history (MySQL client commands and credentials), .python_history (Python REPL statements), and .psql_history (PostgreSQL client commands). Each application records its own command history independently of Bash.

4. grep -oE "[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+" ~/.bash_history | sort -u: the -oE flag prints only the matched portion using extended regular expressions, and sort -u deduplicates the results.

5. sudo -l lists all sudo permissions for the current user. Running it immediately after gaining access reveals whether privilege escalation through sudo is possible and which commands are available.

6. Running cat as root can read any file on the filesystem. That includes /etc/shadow (password hashes for offline cracking), /root/.ssh/id_rsa (root SSH private key for authentication), and /etc/sudoers (sudo policies for all users). Reading these files provides enough credentials and keys to achieve full root access through alternative means.

7. The three priority files are /etc/shadow (password hashes for every account), /root/.ssh/id_rsa (root SSH private key for lateral movement), and /etc/sudoers (sudo policies that may reveal additional misconfigurations or privileged accounts).

8. A root SSH private key authenticates as root on any server that has the matching public key in /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. Organizations often deploy the same key pair across multiple servers. A single stolen private key can grant root access to every server that trusts it, enabling lateral movement across the entire infrastructure without generating password-based authentication logs.

docs.title: Why Malware Analysis Matters
docs.text:
Every intrusion eventually leaves a file behind. A phishing attachment, a dropped loader, a memory-resident beacon, or a binary pulled from a backup: before you can contain an incident, you have to answer a deceptively simple question. What is this thing, and what does it do?

Malware analysis is the discipline of answering that question safely. You do not need a fully equipped reverse-engineering lab to start. You need a quarantine process, a handful of command-line tools, and the discipline to look before you run. This chapter builds those habits from the ground up.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
Seven labs take you from safe sample handling to live command-and-control detection. You will:

  • Triage a quarantined email attachment without executing it
  • Recover an implant's configuration from a memory image with strings
  • Reverse a small Linux agent in Ghidra and read its tasking key off the decompiler
  • Follow HTTP command-and-control streams in a packet capture with Wireshark
  • Detect a live beacon talking to a simulated internet service on INetSim
  • Analyse a phishing email end to end, from authentication headers to the script inside its Word attachment
  • Inspect an OOXML document package, extract an embedded JavaScript beacon, and capture its live C2 traffic

docs.title: How the Labs Work
docs.text:
All seven labs are analyst-side exercises. You work from a REMnux desktop and pull evidence from a dedicated evidence server. The pattern is deliberate:

  1. Launch the exercise and open the REMnux desktop from the panel.
  2. Read the scenario to learn what the SOC already knows.
  3. Pull the evidence from the evidence server with curl.
  4. Analyse the copy. Never execute a recovered sample.
  5. Record indicators and recover the analyst flag.

Safety first. The samples in this chapter are synthetic or harmless by design. The habits are real: work from a copy, hash the original, and never double-click an unknown file. Treat every sample as hostile even when the scenario says it is safe.

docs.title: Connection Details
docs.text:
The evidence server is listed under Target Hostnames on the launch page. Use the IP shown there, or add the hosts entry the panel offers.

Exercise Evidence What you pull 1.1 Evidence server (offset 40) samples.zip (password infected) 1.2 Evidence server (offset 41) svchost.dmp (64 KiB memory image) 1.3 Evidence server (offset 42) halcyon-agent (Linux ELF) 1.4 Evidence server (offset 43) c2-capture.pcap 1.5 INetSim (offset 50), network tap (offset 253) Live PCAP stream on TCP 9999 1.6 Evidence server (offset 44) case-email.eml 1.7 Evidence server (offset 44), INetSim (offset 50), network tap (offset 253) malicious-invoice.docx and the live PCAP stream

Labs 1.1 through 1.4 use a REMnux desktop and the evidence server only. Labs 1.5 and 1.7 add a synthetic victim and an INetSim service; you capture their traffic from the network tap.

docs.title: The Case Files
docs.text:
The chapter follows two organisations.

Northwind Health opens the chapter. An Accounts Payable employee forwards a suspicious invoice attachment, and the SOC quarantines it before anyone opens it. Your job is to confirm what the attachment is and document it for the ticket.

Halcyon Retail Group takes over from Exercise 1.2. An EDR alert on a point-of-sale workstation leads to a memory image, a dropped Linux agent, a packet capture of the beacon, and a live C2 service standing in for the internet. Exercise 1.6 opens a second delivery path, and Exercise 1.7 returns to the same C2 infrastructure through an embedded document script. Each lab adds one more piece of the same intrusion.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
Confirm the following before beginning any lab in this chapter:

  • You can launch an exercise and open the REMnux desktop from the panel
  • You have a terminal open inside REMnux
  • curl, file, strings, sha256sum, and unzip are available
  • Wireshark or tshark is available for Exercises 1.4, 1.5, and 1.7
  • You have read the safe-handling note above

Proceed to Exercise 1.1: Suspicious Attachment Triage when you are ready.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise 1.1 is the first lab in Chapter M1. You will not run the sample. You will identify it, hash it, scan it, and read the analyst note that the SOC left inside the quarantine archive. That sequence is the core of first-line malware triage.

Make sure you have:

  • Launched the exercise and opened the REMnux desktop
  • A terminal open inside REMnux
  • The evidence server IP from Target Hostnames
  • curl, unzip, file, strings, sha256sum, and clamscan available

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Northwind Health runs a small SOC out of their Portland office. An employee in Accounts Payable forwarded an email from billing@northwind-invoices.com with an attached invoice. The attachment was quarantined before anyone opened it, and the on-call analyst dropped it into the team's evidence server.

You are covering the queue this morning. Policy says live samples never travel as loose files: everything sits in a password-protected archive, and the password is the team's standard one. Pull the archive, extract it with the standard password, and triage the sample the way the runbook describes.

The sample is the industry-standard EICAR antivirus test file. It is harmless by design and exists so analysts and AV engines can practise on something that looks malicious without risking a real infection.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Retrieve a quarantined sample without executing it
  • Handle a password-protected sample archive correctly
  • Identify the sample with file, strings, and an antivirus scan
  • Record the sample's size and SHA-256 as indicators of compromise
  • Recover the analyst flag from the archive

docs.title: Background: Why Quarantine Archives Matter
docs.text:
Malware samples are transported inside password-protected ZIP files for two reasons. First, the password stops email gateways and endpoint scanners from opening the archive in transit. Second, it forces a human to make a deliberate decision before the sample is written to disk in a usable form.

The standard password in most malware-handling workflows is infected. It is not a security control. It is a speed bump and a signal that the contents are dangerous.

When you extract a sample, work inside a dedicated directory, keep the archive intact, and record the hash of the extracted file before you do anything else. The hash is the identity of the sample. Two analysts on two machines should get the same value.

docs.title: Tool Primer
docs.text:
Tool What it tells you file The file type based on magic bytes, not the extension sha256sum A stable fingerprint for the sample strings Printable runs inside a binary or text file clamscan Whether an antivirus engine recognises the sample unzip -P Extracts a ZIP with a password

file is always the first command. Extensions lie. A file named invoice.pdf.exe is a Windows executable, and file will say so.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise and Note the Evidence Server
docs.text: Start the lab from the panel and open the REMnux desktop. Under Target Hostnames, note the IP address for evidence.

docs.title: Step 2: Pull the Quarantine Archive
docs.text:
Download the archive onto REMnux

Run this in a REMnux terminal. Replace <evidence_ip> with the address shown on the launch page.

mkdir -p ~/cases/northwind && cd ~/cases/northwind
curl -O http://<evidence_ip>/samples.zip
ls -lh samples.zip

The archive is small. If curl reports a connection error, confirm the evidence server IP and that the lab is still running.

docs.title: Step 3: Inspect the Archive Before Extracting
docs.text:
List the archive contents

unzip -l reads the central directory without extracting anything.

unzip -l samples.zip

You should see two entries: the sample and flag.txt. The -l flag is safe because it does not write the sample to disk.

docs.title: Step 4: Extract With the Standard Password
docs.text:
Extract the quarantine archive

The standard malware-sample password is infected.

unzip -P infected samples.zip
ls -la

You now have the sample and the analyst note in your case directory.

docs.title: Step 5: Identify the Sample
docs.text:
Ask the file what it is

Run file on the extracted sample. Use the exact filename from the archive listing.

file invoice_2026_10.txt

The output should describe a short ASCII text file. That is expected for EICAR: the test string is plain text, not a real executable.

docs.title: Step 6: Hash the Sample
docs.text:
Record the sample fingerprint

sha256sum invoice_2026_10.txt
wc -c invoice_2026_10.txt

Write both values into the ticket. The SHA-256 for the standard EICAR file is a well-known indicator, and the byte count is a quick sanity check.

docs.title: Step 7: Read the Strings
docs.text:
Look at the printable content

strings invoice_2026_10.txt

You should see the EICAR marker. The string is designed to be detected by antivirus engines, so seeing it is the expected result, not an alarm.

docs.title: Step 8: Scan With ClamAV
docs.text:
Run a local antivirus scan

clamscan invoice_2026_10.txt

ClamAV should report a detection. A scanner hit confirms the sample matches a known signature. It does not tell you what the file does, which is why triage combines several tools.

docs.title: Step 9: Recover the Analyst Flag
docs.text:
Read the analyst note

cat flag.txt

Submit the OCR{...} value from the note.

Record Your Findings

  • Sample filename: _______________
  • File type reported by file: _______________
  • Size in bytes: _______________
  • SHA-256: _______________
  • ClamAV result: _______________
  • Analyst flag: _______________

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is the archive password-protected if the sample is harmless?

The password is a handling control, not a containment control for this specific file. It prevents mail gateways and endpoint scanners from opening the archive automatically, and it forces an analyst to extract the sample deliberately. The same workflow is used for real malware, so practising it on EICAR builds the right habit.

2. What does file tell you that the filename does not?

file reads the magic bytes at the start of the file and reports the actual format. The filename is attacker-controlled and can claim to be a PDF, an invoice, or an image. In this case the extension .txt happens to match the content, but the command is still the correct first check.

3. Why record a SHA-256 hash before analysing the sample?

The hash is a stable identity for the exact bytes. It lets other analysts confirm they have the same sample, search threat-intelligence platforms, and compare against known-good or known-bad lists. If the hash changes, the sample has changed, even if the filename is the same.

4. ClamAV detected the file. Does that mean the investigation is over?

No. A signature hit tells you the engine recognises the sample. It does not tell you what the sample does, what it contacts, or whether it is part of a larger intrusion. Triage combines the hash, the file type, the strings, and the scanner result, then hands the sample to deeper analysis if needed.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Never execute a sample to identify it. Start with file, sha256sum, and strings.
  • Password-protected archives are a handling convention. Extract deliberately and keep the original archive intact.
  • The hash is the sample's identity. Record it before you change anything.
  • An antivirus hit is one data point, not a complete analysis.
  • EICAR is safe by design, which makes it a good way to practise the workflow without risking a real infection.

Next: Exercise 1.2; Beacon Configuration Recovery

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise 1.2 picks up the Halcyon Retail Group case. The host was reimaged, so there is no live process to inspect. What survived is a memory image, and your only tool is strings.

Make sure you have:

  • Launched the exercise and opened the REMnux desktop
  • A terminal open inside REMnux
  • The evidence server IP from Target Hostnames
  • curl, file, strings, and grep available

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Halcyon Retail Group's EDR flagged a workstation for a process spawned out of C:\Users\Public that opened outbound TLS to a domain nobody in IT recognised. The on-call analyst isolated the host, but it was reimaged before anyone could attach a debugger. All that survived is a 64 KiB memory image of the process, sitting on the evidence server.

There is no debugger on this box and no time to install one. This is a strings job: pull the dump, let strings pull the printable runs out of it, and read the implant's configuration straight off the page: the C2 address, its user agent, its mutex, and the campaign tag.

The range also plants a single analyst marker in the image, an OCR{...} string. Recover it and submit it.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Retrieve a memory image for analysis without executing anything
  • Use strings to pull printable data out of a binary blob
  • Filter dump noise down to the implant's configuration strings
  • Recover the analyst marker from the image

docs.title: Background: What Lives in a Memory Image
docs.text:
A process memory image is a flat copy of the address space at one moment. It contains code, heap allocations, stack frames, environment strings, and the remnants of anything the process read or wrote. Malware authors often keep configuration as plain strings because it is easy to edit between campaigns: a C2 hostname, a URI path, a user agent, a mutex name, a campaign identifier.

That convenience is also the analyst's advantage. You do not need to disassemble the binary to recover the configuration if it is stored as text. strings walks the file and prints runs of printable characters, typically four or more bytes long, which is enough to surface most configuration values.

The catch is volume. A 64 KiB dump is mostly binary noise and short fragments, so the useful lines are buried. The skill is not running strings; it is filtering the output down to the handful of lines that matter.

docs.title: Tool Primer
docs.text:
Tool What it tells you curl -O Download a file to the current directory file Confirm the container format of the dump strings Printable runs inside a binary blob grep -E Filter those runs with a pattern grep -o Print only the matching part of a line

strings has a minimum-length option (-n). Raising it to 6 or 8 drops short noise and makes the output easier to scan. Lowering it can reveal short values such as mutex names.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise and Note the Evidence Server
docs.text: Start the lab from the panel and open the REMnux desktop. Under Target Hostnames, note the IP address for evidence.

docs.title: Step 2: Pull the Memory Image
docs.text:
Download the dump onto REMnux

mkdir -p ~/cases/halcyon && cd ~/cases/halcyon
curl -O http://<evidence_ip>/svchost.dmp
ls -lh svchost.dmp

The file should be exactly 64 KiB. A different size means the download was truncated; pull it again before analysing.

docs.title: Step 3: Confirm What You Downloaded
docs.text:
Identify the image

file svchost.dmp
sha256sum svchost.dmp

Record the hash in your case notes. The image starts with an MZ header because the process was a Windows executable; the rest is the captured address space.

docs.title: Step 4: Take the First Pass
docs.text:
Dump the printable runs

strings svchost.dmp | less

Do not read top to bottom. Page through and look for short clustered runs: hostnames, paths, mutex names, and identifiers stand out against the random fragments.

docs.title: Step 5: Filter for Configuration Values
docs.text:
Narrow the output

strings svchost.dmp | grep -E 'CFG|https|mutex|campaign'

The implant stores its configuration with a small prefix so the loader can find each value. You should see the C2 host, the beacon path, the user agent, the mutex, and the campaign tag on a handful of lines.

docs.title: Step 6: Extract the Indicators
docs.text:
Pull the values into your notes

strings svchost.dmp | grep -E 'CFG_|mutex|campaign'

Write down each value. These are the indicators you would hand to the detection team: a domain to block, a user agent to alert on, and a mutex to hunt for on other hosts.

docs.title: Step 7: Recover the Analyst Marker
docs.text:
Print only the flag

strings svchost.dmp | grep -o 'OCR{[^}]*}'

If more than one line appears, confirm you are looking at the exact string in the image and not a fragment. Submit the OCR{...} value.

Record Your Findings

  • Image size in bytes: _______________
  • SHA-256: _______________
  • C2 host: _______________
  • Beacon path: _______________
  • User agent: _______________
  • Mutex: _______________
  • Campaign tag: _______________
  • Analyst flag: _______________

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does strings recover configuration that a disassembler would also find, and when is it enough on its own?

Configuration stored as text exists in the image exactly as the author wrote it, so strings can print it without understanding the code. It is enough when the implant keeps its settings as literals. It is not enough when values are built at runtime, encoded, or decrypted; that is the situation in Exercise 1.3, where the key never appears as plaintext.

2. The dump is 64 KiB but only a few lines matter. How do you decide what to keep?

Filter on structure, not on curiosity. Configuration values tend to cluster: a hostname near a path, a user agent near a mutex. Prefixes such as CFG_ make the cluster easy to find. Everything else is noise until it explains a behaviour you already observed, such as the outbound TLS connection in the EDR alert.

3. Why is the campaign tag useful to an investigator even though it is not required to contact the C2?

The tag links samples to a campaign. If the same tag appears on another host or in another image, the analyst can attribute both to the same operator without waiting for the C2 infrastructure to be analysed. It also helps threat-intelligence teams correlate the sample with external reporting.

4. The mutex is not a network indicator. Why record it?

A mutex is a host-based indicator. Malware often creates a named mutex to avoid running twice, and the name is frequently stable across a campaign. A mutex hunt can find infected hosts that are not currently beaconing, which a network indicator alone would miss.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A memory image is a flat snapshot. Configuration strings often survive in it even when the binary is gone.
  • strings is a first-pass tool. Use grep to turn thousands of lines into a handful of indicators.
  • Record the hash before you analyse, and never execute a recovered image.
  • Host-based indicators such as mutexes complement network indicators such as domains and user agents.
  • If the value is not in plaintext, move to code analysis; that is Exercise 1.3.

Next: Exercise 1.3; Agent Reversing in Ghidra

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise 1.3 is the first lab where strings is not enough. The tasking key is built at runtime, so you have to read code. Ghidra is already installed on the REMnux desktop.

Make sure you have:

  • Launched the exercise and opened the REMnux desktop
  • A terminal open inside REMnux
  • The evidence server IP from Target Hostnames
  • At least 4 GB of memory free for Ghidra
  • curl, file, strings, and python3 available

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
The Halcyon Retail Group case moved on. Once the memory image gave up the C2 address, IR went back through the point-of-sale server's backups and found the dropped file itself: halcyon-agent, a small Linux ELF.

The binary will not task without a key. It builds that key at runtime from an obfuscated array and compares whatever you give it against the result. strings shows imports, a banner, and the C2 host you already have, but never the key, and running the file just prints awaiting tasking; the key only exists once the decode routine has run.

The key is also the analyst marker for this case, so recovering it closes two things at once. Open the sample in Ghidra and read the code.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Import an unknown ELF into Ghidra and let auto-analysis run
  • Navigate from main into the tasking validation routine
  • Read a XOR decode loop in the decompiler pane
  • Extract the obfuscated array and its key from the listing
  • Recover the tasking key and submit it

docs.title: Background: Why Runtime Keys Defeat strings
docs.text:
A string literal is stored in the binary exactly as written. If the author puts OCR{...} in the source, strings finds it. If the author stores the bytes XORed with a constant and rebuilds the string at runtime, the plaintext never exists on disk.

Static reversing recovers the plaintext by understanding the rebuild step. You do not need to run the sample. You read the loop, identify the transformation, and apply it yourself. For a single-byte XOR that is a one-line Python script.

This is also why malware analysts prefer static analysis when they can get it: the sample never executes, so there is no risk of detonation and no dependency on the attacker's infrastructure being reachable.

docs.title: Tool Primer
docs.text:
Tool / pane What it shows Ghidra project A container for imported binaries and analysis results CodeBrowser The main disassembly and decompiler window Symbol Tree Functions, labels, and data recovered by analysis Listing Disassembly with addresses, bytes, and operands Decompiler C-like reconstruction of the selected function .rodata Read-only data, where the obfuscated array lives

Ghidra's auto-analysis recovers function boundaries and names from the ELF symbol table. Because this sample is not stripped, main, verify_tasking, and decode_task appear by name, which saves you from hunting through the entry point.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise and Pull the Agent
docs.text:
Download the sample onto REMnux

mkdir -p ~/cases/halcyon && cd ~/cases/halcyon
curl -O http://<evidence_ip>/halcyon-agent
chmod +x halcyon-agent
file halcyon-agent

file should report a 64-bit ELF. Do not run it. The chmod is only so tools that expect an executable bit will open it.

docs.title: Step 2: Confirm the Key Is Not in Plaintext
docs.text:
Check with strings first

strings halcyon-agent | grep -E 'OCR|verify_tasking|cdn-sync'

You will see the function names and the C2 host, but no OCR{...} value. That confirms the key is built at runtime and sends you to the decompiler.

docs.title: Step 3: Start Ghidra and Import the Sample
docs.text:
Create a project and import the ELF

ghidra

In Ghidra:

  1. File > New Project, choose Non-Shared Project, and name it halcyon.
  2. File > Import File and select halcyon-agent.
  3. Accept the detected format (ELF) and click OK.
  4. Accept the default analysis options and click Analyze.

The first import takes a minute or two. Wait for the analysis bar to finish before opening the CodeBrowser.

docs.title: Step 4: Open the CodeBrowser and Find main
docs.text:
Navigate to main

Double-click halcyon-agent in the project tree to open the CodeBrowser. In the Symbol Tree, expand Functions and select main.

The decompiler pane on the right shows the calls main makes. Look for a call to verify_tasking.

docs.title: Step 5: Follow the Validation Routine
docs.text:
Open verify_tasking

Double-click verify_tasking in the decompiler pane (or select it in the Symbol Tree). The function calls decode_task with four arguments: a destination buffer, the obfuscated array, its length, and the key byte.

Note the name of the array argument, typically task_blob, and the key byte passed alongside it.

docs.title: Step 6: Read the Obfuscated Array
docs.text:
Inspect task_blob in the listing

Click task_blob in the decompiler or listing. Ghidra jumps to the bytes in .rodata. They look like random data because they are XORed with the key.

You do not need to transcribe them by hand. Either read them in the listing or pull the same bytes out of the file with python3 once you know the offset.

docs.title: Step 7: Reproduce the Decode Loop
docs.text:
XOR the array with the key

The loop applies a single-byte XOR. The key byte is the fourth argument to decode_task. With the key in hand, the whole array decodes to the tasking string:

python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
data = Path('halcyon-agent').read_bytes()
# Replace 0x6b with the key byte you read from verify_tasking.
decoded = bytes(b ^ 0x6b for b in data)
start = decoded.find(b'OCR{')
end = decoded.find(b'}', start)
print(decoded[start:end + 1].decode())
PY

The output is the tasking key. It is also the analyst marker for the case.

docs.title: Step 8: Submit the Key
docs.text:
Record and submit

Write the key into the case notes and submit the OCR{...} value.

Record Your Findings

  • File type: _______________
  • Architecture: _______________
  • Obfuscated array name: _______________
  • Key byte: _______________
  • Decode routine: _______________
  • Tasking key: _______________

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does strings fail on this sample when it worked in Exercise 1.2?

The configuration in Exercise 1.2 was stored as plain text. Here the key is stored as ciphertext and rebuilt at runtime by decode_task. strings only prints bytes that are already printable, so it cannot recover a value that only exists after the XOR loop runs.

2. What does the decompiler give you that the disassembly alone does not?

The decompiler reconstructs control flow and data flow into C-like code. You can see that verify_tasking passes four arguments to decode_task and that the fourth is the key byte, without tracing register moves by hand. The disassembly remains authoritative when the decompiler output is ambiguous.

3. Could you recover the key by running the sample instead?

Possibly, but you should not. Running unknown malware risks detonation, persistence, and outbound contact with live infrastructure. Static analysis recovers the same value without executing a single instruction. In an investigation, the safe path is also the reproducible path.

4. Why keep the symbol names in a real implant?

Most malware is stripped, and this sample is not, which is a deliberate teaching choice. Symbols make the first reversing exercise about reading code rather than about locating main. In a real case, you would start from the entry point and work outward, using imports and string cross-references as anchors.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A value that never appears as plaintext on disk is a job for the decompiler, not strings.
  • Follow the call graph from main. Function names and imports are anchors.
  • Single-byte XOR is trivial to reverse once you have the key byte and the array.
  • Static analysis keeps the sample from executing while still recovering the secret.
  • Record the key byte and the decode routine; they explain the finding and let another analyst reproduce it.

Next: Exercise 1.4; C2 Traffic in Wireshark

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise 1.4 moves from the sample to the wire. You have the C2 domain and the beacon path from the earlier labs; now you have to prove the beacon actually ran by reading a packet capture.

Make sure you have:

  • Launched the exercise and opened the REMnux desktop
  • A terminal open inside REMnux
  • The evidence server IP from Target Hostnames
  • Wireshark available in the desktop menu, and tshark in the terminal
  • The C2 domain from Exercise 1.2 in your notes

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Halcyon Retail Group's network team pulled a span-port capture from the segment that served the point-of-sale workstation. The host has been rebuilt and the agent is gone, but the capture still holds the conversation between the implant and its command-and-control server.

The capture is small on purpose: one beacon cycle, plus enough background traffic to make you filter. Your job is to reconstruct the beacon, identify the C2 host and URI, and recover the task key the server handed back.

The task key is the analyst marker for this lab. It appears in the HTTP response, which is unencrypted in this capture.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Open a packet capture and identify the protocols in use
  • Filter HTTP traffic down to the C2 conversation
  • Follow a TCP stream and read the request and response
  • Extract the beacon URI, user agent, and task key
  • Recover the analyst marker from the response body

docs.title: Background: What a Beacon Looks Like on the Wire
docs.text:
A beacon is a repeating outbound request. The implant checks in on a schedule, receives tasking, and goes quiet until the next interval. On the wire the pattern is a small HTTP request to an unusual host, often with a plausible but generic user agent, followed by a short response.

Analysts look for four things:

  1. Destination - a domain or IP that is not part of normal business traffic.
  2. Cadence - requests at regular intervals, often with jitter.
  3. URI shape - a path that looks like an API endpoint but is not one you recognise.
  4. Response content - tasking, keys, or configuration returned to the implant.

This capture contains one cycle. In a longer capture you would also measure the interval between requests; here you reconstruct a single exchange and record the indicators.

docs.title: Tool Primer
docs.text:
Tool / filter What it does http Show only HTTP requests and responses http.request Show only requests http.host contains "..." Filter by Host header tcp.stream eq N Isolate one TCP conversation Follow > TCP Stream Reassemble the full request and response tshark -r file -Y "..." Apply a display filter from the terminal tshark -r file -T fields -e http.request.uri Extract a field

If the capture uses a non-standard port, Wireshark may not decode it as HTTP automatically. Right-click a packet and choose Decode As > HTTP if the request appears as raw TCP.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise and Pull the Capture
docs.text:
Download the PCAP onto REMnux

mkdir -p ~/cases/halcyon && cd ~/cases/halcyon
curl -O http://<evidence_ip>/c2-capture.pcap
ls -lh c2-capture.pcap
file c2-capture.pcap

file should report a pcap capture file. Record the SHA-256 before you open it, the same as any other piece of evidence.

docs.title: Step 2: Get the Protocol Overview
docs.text:
Summarise the capture

capinfos c2-capture.pcap
tshark -r c2-capture.pcap -q -z io,phs

You should see Ethernet, IPv4, TCP, DNS, and HTTP. The presence of DNS tells you the victim resolved a name before connecting, which is useful: the query itself is an indicator.

docs.title: Step 3: Find the Suspicious Conversation
docs.text:
List HTTP requests

tshark -r c2-capture.pcap -Y http.request \
  -T fields -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e http.host -e http.request.uri -e http.user_agent

One request should stand out: a host that is not a normal business service, a URI that looks like an API endpoint, and a user agent that does not match the operating system.

docs.title: Step 4: Open the Capture in Wireshark
docs.text:
Filter to the C2 host

wireshark c2-capture.pcap &

Apply the display filter:

http.host contains "cdn-sync-update.com"

You should see the request and the response. If the filter returns nothing, check the exact host in the tshark output from Step 3.

docs.title: Step 5: Follow the TCP Stream
docs.text:
Read the full exchange

Right-click the request packet and choose Follow > TCP Stream. The stream window shows the request headers, the response headers, and the response body in order.

Read the request line and the Host header first. Then read the response. The body is JSON tasking and contains the task key.

docs.title: Step 6: Extract the Indicators
docs.text:
Pull the fields you need for the ticket

tshark -r c2-capture.pcap -Y http.request \
  -T fields -e http.host -e http.request.uri -e http.user_agent

Record the C2 host, the beacon URI, and the user agent. These are the network indicators the detection team needs.

docs.title: Step 7: Recover the Analyst Marker
docs.text:
Print the task key

tshark -r c2-capture.pcap -Y http.response \
  -T fields -e http.file_data | tr -d '\\n' | grep -o 'OCR{[^}]*}'

If http.file_data is empty, the response may be split across segments. Use Follow > TCP Stream and copy the value from the body, or fall back to:

strings c2-capture.pcap | grep -o 'OCR{[^}]*}'

Submit the OCR{...} value.

Record Your Findings

  • Capture SHA-256: _______________
  • Victim IP: _______________
  • C2 host: _______________
  • C2 IP: _______________
  • Beacon URI: _______________
  • User agent: _______________
  • Task key: _______________

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. The capture is HTTP, not HTTPS. Why does that matter for this exercise, and what would change if it were TLS?

Plain HTTP exposes the request line, headers, and body, so you can read the beacon URI and the task key directly. If the beacon used TLS, you would see the destination and the timing but not the content, and you would need endpoint telemetry, a TLS key log, or a TLS-intercepting proxy to recover the body. The detection value of the destination and cadence would remain.

2. Why is the DNS query an indicator even though the HTTP request is the actual beacon?

The DNS query reveals the domain before the connection is made, and it may be the only visible artifact if the HTTP connection fails or is blocked. It also maps the domain to the C2 IP, which lets you build a block list for both. In this capture the query and the request agree, which strengthens the finding.

3. How would you distinguish this beacon from a legitimate software update check?

Legitimate update checks usually go to a vendor domain with a documented user agent and a stable, well-known URI. This request goes to an unrecognised domain with an API-shaped path and a generic user agent. Context matters too: the host had an EDR alert, and the domain does not appear in the organisation's allow list.

4. What would you do with the user agent after this lab?

Add it to the detection platform as a low-confidence signature. It is easy for an attacker to change, so it should not be the only rule, but it can catch other hosts running the same implant before they are identified by behaviour. Pair it with the domain and URI for a higher-confidence composite rule.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A beacon is a repeating outbound request. Destination, cadence, URI shape, and response content are the four things to record.
  • Filter first, then follow the stream. Filters find the conversation; the stream explains it.
  • DNS is part of the story, not background noise.
  • Plain HTTP exposes tasking and keys; TLS hides them but not the destination or timing.
  • Indicators from the wire complement the host indicators from Exercises 1.2 and 1.3.

Next: Exercise 1.5; Detecting C2 to INetSim

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise 1.5 is the live version of Exercise 1.4. Instead of a static capture, you watch a synthetic victim beacon to a simulated internet service and capture the traffic yourself.

Make sure you have:

  • Launched the exercise and opened the REMnux desktop
  • A terminal open inside REMnux
  • The C2 Service and Network Tap addresses from the panel
  • nc, tcpdump, and Wireshark available
  • The C2 domain and beacon URI from the earlier labs

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Halcyon Retail Group has rebuilt the point-of-sale workstation and put it on an isolated segment with a simulated internet service. The rebuild restored a backup that still contained the implant, so the beacon is running again; this time the SOC can watch it happen.

INetSim stands in for the internet. It answers DNS for any domain and serves fake files for common extensions, which is exactly what an isolated range needs to let a beacon believe it reached its C2. A network tap mirrors the segment and streams the packets to you as a live PCAP.

Your job is to capture the beacon, prove it is command-and-control rather than legitimate update traffic, and recover the task key the fake C2 returns.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Connect to the network tap and stream live packets to a capture file
  • Identify the synthetic victim and the simulated C2 service
  • Capture a full beacon cycle, including the DNS lookup and the HTTP exchange
  • Read the request and response from the live capture
  • Recover the analyst marker from the C2 response

docs.title: Background: INetSim and Why Ranges Use It
docs.text:
INetSim is a network service simulator. It listens for DNS, HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, FTP, and other protocols and answers as if it were a real server. In a range it serves two purposes:

  1. Containment. Malware that beacons out never reaches the real internet.
  2. Observability. The simulator logs every request, and the traffic stays on the lab bridge where a tap can capture it.

By default INetSim answers DNS with its own address, so any domain the victim resolves points back at the simulator. HTTP fake mode then returns a fake file based on the requested extension. The range configures a json fake file so the beacon's API request returns tasking that contains the analyst marker.

The network tap is a separate container that mirrors all traffic on the lab bridge and streams it as PCAP over TCP port 9999. You connect, and tcpdump or Wireshark reads the stream.

docs.title: Tool Primer
docs.text:
Tool / filter What it does nc <tap> 9999 Connect to the live PCAP stream tcpdump -r - -nn Read a PCAP stream from stdin tcpdump -i eth0 Capture on an interface -w file.pcap Write packets to a file http.host contains "..." Filter by Host header in Wireshark dns.qry.name contains "..." Filter DNS queries by name

The tap streams a PCAP file, not raw packets, so tcpdump -r - and Wireshark can read it directly. Write it to a file first if you want to analyse it after the connection closes.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch the Exercise and Note the Addresses
docs.text:
Start the lab from the panel and open the REMnux desktop. Under Target Hostnames, note:

  • c2-service - the INetSim host (offset 50)
  • victim - the synthetic workstation (offset 51)
  • network-tap - the capture stream (offset 253)

The tap is not a target you attack. It is a sensor.

docs.title: Step 2: Start a Capture
docs.text:
Stream the tap to a file

mkdir -p ~/cases/halcyon && cd ~/cases/halcyon
timeout 40 nc <network-tap> 9999 > live-c2.pcap
ls -lh live-c2.pcap

The command blocks for 40 seconds while the tap streams packets. Let it run through at least one beacon interval. If nc exits immediately, confirm the tap address and that the exercise is still running.

To watch in real time instead, pipe the stream into tcpdump:

nc <network-tap> 9999 | tcpdump -r - -nn -A 'port 80'

docs.title: Step 3: Confirm the Capture Is Valid
docs.text:
Summarise the live capture

capinfos live-c2.pcap
tshark -r live-c2.pcap -q -z io,phs

You should see DNS and HTTP between the victim and the C2 service. If the capture is empty, the beacon may not have fired during the window; capture for longer.

docs.title: Step 4: Find the Beacon
docs.text:
List HTTP requests from the victim

tshark -r live-c2.pcap -Y http.request \
  -T fields -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e http.host -e http.request.uri -e http.user_agent

The victim should be requesting the C2 domain at the API path you recorded in Exercise 1.4. The destination IP is the INetSim service, not the real internet.

docs.title: Step 5: Read the Exchange
docs.text:
Follow the stream

wireshark live-c2.pcap &

Apply http.host contains "cdn-sync-update.com", then right-click the request and choose Follow > TCP Stream. Read the request and the JSON response. The response is the fake tasking from INetSim.

docs.title: Step 6: Prove It Is C2, Not an Update
docs.text:
Compare behaviour with a legitimate update

tshark -r live-c2.pcap -Y dns \
  -T fields -e dns.qry.name | sort -u

A legitimate update check goes to a vendor domain with a documented user agent and a stable URI. This beacon goes to an unrecognised domain, uses an API-shaped path, and repeats on a short interval. Record the cadence if you captured more than one cycle.

docs.title: Step 7: Recover the Analyst Marker
docs.text:
Extract the task key

tshark -r live-c2.pcap -Y http.response \
  -T fields -e http.file_data | tr -d '\\n' | grep -o 'OCR{[^}]*}'

If the response is split across segments, use Follow > TCP Stream and copy the value from the JSON body, or fall back to:

strings live-c2.pcap | grep -o 'OCR{[^}]*}'

Submit the OCR{...} value.

Record Your Findings

  • Capture SHA-256: _______________
  • Victim IP: _______________
  • C2 service IP: _______________
  • C2 domain: _______________
  • Beacon URI: _______________
  • Beacon interval: _______________
  • Task key: _______________

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does INetSim answer DNS for a domain it does not own?

INetSim is a simulator, not a resolver. Its job is to make the range look like the internet to a sample that expects one. It answers any query with its own address so the sample connects back to the simulator instead of leaving the lab. That containment is the point.

2. How does the network tap differ from running tcpdump on the victim?

The tap mirrors traffic on the lab bridge, so it sees every container's conversation without installing tools on the victim. Running tcpdump on the victim would only show that host's traffic and would require access to a host you may not control. The tap is an out-of-band sensor.

3. The beacon repeats on a fixed interval. Why is cadence a strong detection signal?

Fixed-interval outbound requests to the same destination are unusual for human-driven traffic and common for implants. Cadence survives changes to the domain and user agent, so a detection built on timing can catch a beacon even after the operator rotates infrastructure. Jitter weakens the signal, which is why analysts combine cadence with destination and URI shape.

4. What would you block first: the domain, the IP, or the URI?

The domain is the most durable indicator for this campaign, but it is also the easiest for the operator to change. The IP is specific to this range and would be the simulator address, not a real one. The URI is useful for a composite rule. In a real incident you would block the domain and IP at the perimeter and add the URI and user agent to detection, then hunt for the same pattern on other hosts.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• INetSim simulates the internet so a beacon can run safely inside the range.
  • The tap is an out-of-band sensor; you do not need to instrument the victim.
  • A live capture lets you measure cadence, which a single-cycle PCAP cannot show.
  • The same four indicators apply: destination, cadence, URI shape, response content.
  • Containment and observability are the reasons ranges use simulated services.

Next: Exercise 1.6; Email Attachment Analysis

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise 1.6 returns to where most intrusions start: an email. This time the message is intact, so you can analyse both the delivery path and the attachment.

Make sure you have:

  • Launched the exercise and opened the REMnux desktop
  • A terminal open inside REMnux
  • The Evidence Server address from the panel
  • python3, curl, grep, and base64 available
  • Read the safety notes from Exercise 1.1

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Halcyon Retail Group's accounts payable team reported an overdue-invoice email. The message looks routine, but the sender domain, the reply-to address, and the authentication results do not agree.

The attachment is named Invoice_INV-88213.doc. It is not a real Word document: it is HTML with a JScript block, a common trick for getting script past file-type filters. The script builds a marker, but one piece of that marker lives in the message headers rather than in the attachment.

Your job is to analyse the message as delivered, extract the attachment safely, and assemble the analyst flag from both halves.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Read the message headers and identify the sender/reply-to mismatch
  • Interpret SPF, DKIM, and DMARC results from Authentication-Results
  • Extract the .doc attachment from the MIME structure without opening it
  • Inspect the document's JavaScript and locate the marker fragment
  • Combine the header token with the JavaScript fragment to recover the flag

docs.title: Background: Headers Tell the Delivery Story
docs.text:
An email has two layers. The envelope is what the mail servers exchange: Return-Path, the sending IP, and the recipient. The headers are what the message carries: From, Reply-To, Subject, Message-ID, and the authentication results added by the receiving mail server.

Attackers can set most headers to anything they like. They cannot set the receiving server's authentication results. That is why those results are the first thing an analyst reads.

Header What it tells you From The display identity the user sees. Trivially spoofed. Return-Path Where bounces go. Often a different domain from From. Reply-To Where replies go. A mismatch here is a classic phishing signal. Received The path the message took. Read bottom-up. Authentication-Results SPF, DKIM, and DMARC verdicts added by the receiver. Received-SPF The SPF check result in more detail. Message-ID The sending system's identifier. Its domain should match the sender. X-Originating-IP The client IP, when the sender's mail system records it.

docs.title: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC in one paragraph each
docs.text:
SPF asks whether the sending IP is allowed to send for the envelope domain. A fail means the message came from an IP the domain did not authorise.

DKIM is a cryptographic signature over selected headers and the body. A none result means there was no signature to check.

DMARC ties SPF and DKIM to the visible From domain and tells the receiver what to do when both fail. A dmarc=fail with spf=fail and dkim=none is a strong delivery-path indicator.

None of these prove a message is malicious on their own. Together they tell you the message did not legitimately come from the domain it claims.

docs.title: Background: MIME and the HTML-as-Word Trick
docs.text:
A modern email is a MIME tree. multipart/mixed holds the body plus attachments. Each part has its own Content-Type, Content-Disposition, and Content-Transfer-Encoding.

The attachment in this case claims application/msword and a .doc filename, but its bytes are HTML. Windows often opens the file in a browser or a Word HTML view, where the script can run. Analysts read the part as text instead.

Never double-click the attachment. Extract the part, decode it, and inspect the source.

docs.title: Tool Primer
docs.text:
Tool / field What it does curl -o case.eml Save the raw message with headers intact grep -i '^Header:' Print one header without decoding the body grep -c 'dmarc=fail' Count authentication failures python3 -m email Parse the MIME tree base64 -d Decode a single transfer-encoded part strings Quick look at printable content

Python's email module is the reliable way to walk the tree. It handles folded headers, quoted-printable, and base64 for you.

docs.title: Step 1: Pull the Message
docs.text:
Download the raw message

curl -s http://<evidence>/case-email.eml -o case.eml
ls -l case.eml

Keep the file exactly as served. Opening it in a mail client can rewrite headers and hide the delivery path.

docs.title: Step 2: Read the Delivery Headers
docs.text:
Print the headers that matter

grep -iE '^(From|Return-Path|Reply-To|Received|Authentication-Results|Received-SPF|Message-ID|X-Originating-IP|X-OCR-Case-Token):' case.eml

Read the result carefully:

  • Does From match Return-Path?
  • Does Reply-To point somewhere unexpected?
  • What do SPF, DKIM, and DMARC say?
  • Does the Message-ID domain match the sender?

The X-OCR-Case-Token header is unusual by design. It carries the first half of the analyst marker. Note the value; you will need it in Step 5.

docs.title: Step 3: Interpret the Authentication Chain
docs.text:
Count the failures

grep -c 'dmarc=fail' case.eml
grep -i 'Received-SPF' case.eml

A single failed check can be a misconfiguration. A failed SPF, absent DKIM, and failed DMARC together mean the message did not come from the domain it claims. Combined with the lookalike Reply-To, that is enough to quarantine the message and start attachment analysis.

docs.title: Step 4: Extract the Attachment Safely
docs.text:
Walk the MIME tree

python3 - <<'PY'
import email, base64

msg = email.message_from_bytes(open("case.eml", "rb").read())
for part in msg.walk():
    name = part.get_filename()
    if not name:
        continue
    print("attachment:", name, part.get_content_type())
    data = part.get_payload(decode=True)
    open("/tmp/" + name, "wb").write(data)
    print("bytes:", len(data))
PY

The output should show one attachment, Invoice_INV-88213.doc, with type application/msword. Confirm what it really is:

file /tmp/Invoice_INV-88213.doc
head -c 200 /tmp/Invoice_INV-88213.doc

The first bytes are HTML, not the OLE compound-file magic (D0 CF 11 E0).

docs.title: Step 5: Inspect the JavaScript
docs.text:
Read the document as text

grep -n -A 12 -i 'script' /tmp/Invoice_INV-88213.doc

You will find a JScript block that builds a marker:

var headerToken = "REPLACE_WITH_X-OCR-CASE-TOKEN";
var stage = "h34d3rs_4nd_w0rd_js}";
var marker = "OCR{" + headerToken + stage;

The stage variable is the second half of the flag. The first half is the X-OCR-Case-Token header value from Step 2. The script deliberately does not contain the header token: the attachment alone is not enough.

docs.title: Step 6: Assemble and Submit the Flag
docs.text:
Combine OCR{, the header token, and the stage value:

OCR{ + <X-OCR-Case-Token> + <stage>

Submit the completed flag in the exercise panel. Before you move on, write the indicators into your case notes:

  • Sending IP and Return-Path domain
  • Reply-To lookalike domain
  • Authentication verdicts
  • Attachment name, true type, and script behaviour

docs.title: Defensive Takeaways
docs.text:
The same facts you extracted are the controls a defender can act on:

  • Authentication enforcement. A DMARC policy of reject with SPF and DKIM aligned would have stopped this message at the gateway. The dmarc=fail verdict in the headers is the signal to act on.
  • Reply-To scrutiny. Flag messages where Reply-To uses a different domain than From, especially a lookalike. Many mail gateways expose this as a rule.
  • Attachment type, not extension. Inspect the real content type and magic bytes of attachments. A .doc that is actually HTML should never reach the user.
  • Script blocking. Disable HTML/ActiveX rendering in mail previews and block JScript execution from the temp directory.
  • User reporting. The fastest detection came from the user. A one-click report button plus a SOC triage queue turns that into a control.

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Answer these in your own words before checking the review.

  1. Which header is the strongest evidence that the message did not come from halcyon-retail.com? Why can the attacker not simply forge it?
  2. Why is a Reply-To mismatch more useful to an analyst than a suspicious display name?
  3. What does the attachment's true file type tell you about the sender's goal, and why would HTML be chosen over a real macro-enabled document?
  4. Why is it safer to parse the MIME tree with Python than to open the attachment in a word processor?
  5. The JavaScript references the header token but does not store it. What does that design suggest about how the message and attachment were produced?
  6. Which single control would have stopped this message before it reached the user's inbox?

docs.title: Indicators to Record
docs.text: Indicator Example from this case Sender IP 203.0.113.47 Envelope domain halcyon-retail.co Reply-To it-support@halcyon-retail.co Authentication spf=fail, dkim=none, dmarc=fail Attachment Invoice_INV-88213.doc (HTML + JScript) Subject lure Overdue invoice, urgent action

docs.title: If You Get Stuck
docs.text:
• No attachment found: print part.get_content_type() for every part, not just the ones with filenames.
  • The decoded file looks empty: use get_payload(decode=True) rather than get_payload(); the part is base64-encoded.
  • The flag is short: you probably used only the JavaScript half. The header token comes first.
  • Header lines wrap: use Python's msg.get("Header-Name") to let the parser unfold them.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
Exercise 1.7 takes the same delivery-path question one layer deeper: the attachment is a real OOXML package with an embedded JavaScript object. You will list the package parts, extract the script, and capture the beacon it describes against INetSim.

The Chapter Review brings together the handling discipline, static analysis, network analysis, and delivery-path triage you practised across all seven labs.

Next: Exercise 1.7; Embedded JavaScript C2 in Documents

docs.title: Exercise 1.7: Embedded JavaScript C2 in Documents
Before You Begin
docs.text:
Exercise 1.7 returns to the delivery path one more time. This document is a real Office Open XML package, and the payload is an embedded JavaScript object rather than a macro. You will inspect the package without opening Word, identify the beacon configuration, and then capture the live traffic.

Make sure you have:

  • Launched the exercise and opened the REMnux desktop
  • A terminal open inside REMnux
  • The Evidence Server, C2 Service, and Network Tap addresses from the panel
  • curl, unzip, python3, strings, and tshark available
  • Read the safety notes from Exercise 1.1

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Halcyon Retail Group's finance team reported an invoice attachment that triggered an outbound connection from a workstation. The message looked like a routine remittance notice, but the attached DOCX contains an embedded JavaScript object that beacons to a command-and-control service.

The synthetic victim has the document and is running the same beacon loop the script describes. INetSim stands in for the internet: it answers DNS for the C2 domain and serves the fake tasking endpoint. A network tap mirrors the segment and streams the packets to you as a live PCAP.

Your job is to pull the document from the evidence server, extract the embedded script, identify the C2 configuration, and capture the beacon to recover the task key.

docs.title: Your Objectives
docs.text:
• Extract the embedded JavaScript from the malicious Word document
  • Identify the C2 domain, beacon URI, and check-in interval in the script
  • Capture the live beacon from the network tap
  • Recover the task key from the C2 response

docs.title: Background: A DOCX Is a ZIP Package
docs.text:
A modern Word document is not a single binary file. It is an Office Open XML (OOXML) package: a ZIP archive containing XML parts, relationships, and optionally embedded objects. Rename a DOCX to .zip and you can inspect every part without a word processor.

The parts that matter in this exercise:

Part Purpose [Content_Types].xml Declares the content type of each part _rels/.rels Points the package at the main document part word/document.xml The visible document text word/_rels/document.xml.rels Relationships from the document to other parts word/embeddings/beacon.js The embedded script object

An embedded object is referenced by a relationship. The document text can look completely ordinary while the relationship points at a script that runs when the object is activated.

docs.title: Why embedded JavaScript instead of a macro?
docs.text: Macro-enabled formats such as .docm are widely blocked and inspected. OOXML packages can carry other object types, including scriptlets and embedded packages, and the extension still looks like an ordinary document. The defence is the same: inspect the package structure, not just the file extension.

docs.title: Tool Primer
docs.text:
Tool / command What it does file invoice.docx Confirms the ZIP/OOXML container unzip -l invoice.docx Lists package parts without extracting unzip -p invoice.docx <part> Prints one part to stdout python3 -m zipfile -l invoice.docx Lists parts when unzip is unavailable strings Quick look at printable content olevba invoice.docx Confirms whether VBA macros are present tshark -r capture.pcap -Y http.request Filters HTTP requests in a capture

unzip -p is the safest way to read a part: it writes to stdout and leaves no extracted copy behind.

docs.title: Step 1: Pull the Document
docs.text:
Download the attachment

mkdir -p ~/cases/halcyon-doc && cd ~/cases/halcyon-doc
curl -s http://<evidence>/malicious-invoice.docx -o invoice.docx
ls -lh invoice.docx
file invoice.docx

file should identify a Microsoft Word 2007+ document. Record the SHA-256 before you inspect it:

sha256sum invoice.docx

docs.title: Step 2: List the Package Parts
docs.text:
Inspect the OOXML structure

unzip -l invoice.docx

Look for the word/embeddings/ directory. A document that claims to be a simple invoice rarely needs an embedded object.

If unzip is not available, use Python's standard library:

python3 -m zipfile -l invoice.docx

docs.title: Step 3: Extract the Embedded Script
docs.text:
Read the script without opening Word

unzip -p invoice.docx word/embeddings/beacon.js

You should see a JavaScript object with the C2 configuration. Write down:

  • the C2 domain
  • the task URI
  • the check-in interval
  • any session or campaign identifier

The script does not contain the task key. The key is returned by the C2 service when the beacon checks in.

docs.title: Step 4: Confirm There Are No Macros
docs.text:
Check the macro surface

olevba invoice.docx

olevba should report that the file contains no VBA macros. That is the point: the payload is not a macro, so a macro-only inspection would miss it. The embedded object is the finding.

docs.title: Step 5: Start a Capture
docs.text:
Stream the network tap to a file

timeout 40 nc <network-tap> 9999 > doc-c2.pcap
ls -lh doc-c2.pcap

The command blocks for 40 seconds. The victim checks in every ten seconds, so that window should contain several beacon cycles. If the capture is empty, confirm the tap address and that the exercise is still running.

To watch in real time instead:

nc <network-tap> 9999 | tcpdump -r - -nn -A 'port 80'

docs.title: Step 6: Find the Beacon
docs.text:
Filter the HTTP requests

tshark -r doc-c2.pcap -Y http.request \
  -T fields -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e http.host -e http.request.uri -e http.user_agent

The victim should be requesting the C2 domain and the task URI you found in the script. The destination is the INetSim service, not the real internet.

Confirm the DNS lookup as well:

tshark -r doc-c2.pcap -Y dns \
  -T fields -e dns.qry.name | sort -u

docs.title: Step 7: Read the Response and Recover the Task Key
docs.text:
Follow the exchange

wireshark doc-c2.pcap &

Apply http.host contains "cdn-sync-update.com", right-click the request, and choose Follow > TCP Stream. The JSON response is the fake tasking from INetSim.

You can also extract the key directly:

tshark -r doc-c2.pcap -Y http.response \
  -T fields -e http.file_data | tr -d '\n' | grep -o 'OCR{[^}]*}'

If the response is split across segments, fall back to:

strings doc-c2.pcap | grep -o 'OCR{[^}]*}'

Submit the OCR{...} value.

Record Your Findings

  • Document SHA-256: _______________
  • Embedded object: _______________
  • C2 domain: _______________
  • Task URI: _______________
  • Beacon interval: _______________
  • Session identifier: _______________
  • Victim IP: _______________
  • C2 service IP: _______________
  • Task key: _______________

docs.title: Analysis Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does a DOCX with no macros still deserve package-level inspection?
  2. What does the relationship in word/_rels/document.xml.rels tell you that the visible text in word/document.xml does not?
  3. Why is unzip -p safer than extracting the package into your working directory?
  4. What three configuration values in the script would let you write a network detection rule?
  5. Why does the script not contain the task key?
  6. How would the capture differ if the C2 endpoint used TLS instead of plain HTTP?

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A DOCX is a ZIP package. Inspect the parts, not just the extension.
  • Embedded objects are referenced through relationships and can carry script without any VBA macro.
  • The beacon configuration lives in the script; the task key lives in the C2 response.
  • A live capture lets you confirm the domain, URI, cadence, and response in one place.
  • Macro-only inspection is not enough for modern document-borne payloads.

Next: Chapter M1 Review

docs.title: What You Learned
docs.text:
Over seven labs you followed one intrusion from a quarantined email attachment to a live command-and-control beacon, then closed the loop with an email that started another and a document whose embedded script pointed back at the same kind of infrastructure. The samples changed, the tools changed, and the evidence changed, but the analytical method stayed the same:

  1. Acquire the evidence without executing it.
  2. Identify what you have before you analyse it.
  3. Start with the cheapest technique that can answer the question.
  4. Escalate to code analysis or live capture only when the cheap technique cannot.
  5. Record indicators in a form another analyst can act on.

By the final lab you were extracting a payload from an Office package, identifying its beacon configuration, and proving from a live capture that the traffic was command-and-control rather than a legitimate update check.

docs.text:
graph LR
    A["1.1 EICAR Triage"] --> B["1.2 Strings Analysis"]
    B --> C["1.3 Ghidra Reversing"]
    C --> D["1.4 C2 PCAP"]
    D --> E["1.5 Live INetSim C2"]
    E --> F["1.6 Email Attachment"]
    F --> G["1.7 Embedded JS Document"]
    style A fill:#f59e0b,color:#1f2937
    style G fill:#6aaa64,color:#fff
Exercise Evidence Technique What You Recovered 1.1 samples.zip Quarantine handling, file, sha256sum, clamscan Sample identity and analyst note 1.2 svchost.dmp strings, grep C2 host, user agent, mutex, campaign tag 1.3 halcyon-agent Ghidra decompiler, XOR Runtime tasking key 1.4 c2-capture.pcap Wireshark, tshark Beacon URI, C2 IP, task key 1.5 Live tap stream nc, tcpdump, Wireshark Live beacon and task key 1.6 case-email.eml Header analysis, MIME parsing, JavaScript review Header token plus attachment marker 1.7 malicious-invoice.docx OOXML package inspection, unzip, live capture Embedded script configuration and task key

Each lab built on the last:

  • Exercise 1.1 established the handling discipline. You never executed the sample, and you recorded a hash before analysis.
  • Exercise 1.2 showed how much configuration survives in memory and how far strings can take you.
  • Exercise 1.3 showed the limit of strings and introduced static code analysis as the next step.
  • Exercise 1.4 moved from the host to the wire and taught you to read a beacon from a capture.
  • Exercise 1.5 made the capture live and added containment through INetSim and observation through a network tap.
  • Exercise 1.6 returned to the delivery path and showed how headers and an attachment can each hold half of the answer. It also reinforced the rule that an attachment's extension is not its type.
  • Exercise 1.7 opened the document package itself and showed that a DOCX can carry script without a VBA macro. It combined static configuration recovery with the live-capture skills from Exercise 1.5.

docs.title: Self-Assessment
docs.text:
Answer these questions without looking at the answer key below. If you can answer all nine confidently, you have internalised the core skills of this chapter. If any question gives you trouble, revisit the corresponding lab.

  1. Why do malware samples travel in password-protected ZIP files, and what is the standard password? (Exercise 1.1)

  2. What does file tell you that a filename does not? (Exercise 1.1)

  3. What is the difference between a network indicator and a host-based indicator? Give one example of each from Exercise 1.2. (Exercise 1.2)

  4. Why does strings fail to recover a runtime-built key? (Exercise 1.3)

  5. What are the four things an analyst records about a beacon? (Exercise 1.4)

  6. Why does INetSim answer DNS for domains it does not own? (Exercise 1.5)

  7. What does the network tap give you that tcpdump on the victim does not? (Exercise 1.5)

  8. Why should you read the authentication headers before opening an attachment, and what did the attachment's true file type reveal? (Exercise 1.6)

  9. Why can a DOCX carry executable script without containing a VBA macro, and which package part tells you where the script is? (Exercise 1.7)

docs.title: Answer Key
docs.text:
1. The password prevents mail gateways and endpoint scanners from opening the archive automatically and forces a deliberate extraction decision. The standard password is infected.

2. file reads the magic bytes and reports the actual format. A filename is attacker-controlled and can claim to be a PDF or an image when the content is an executable.

3. A network indicator is observable on the wire, such as the C2 host cdn-sync-update.com or the beacon URI. A host-based indicator lives on the endpoint, such as the mutex name or the file path the process ran from. Both belong in the case notes because they support different hunts.

4. The plaintext never exists on disk. The bytes are stored XORed with a key and rebuilt only when the decode routine runs, so strings sees ciphertext.

5. Destination, cadence, URI shape, and response content.

6. INetSim is a simulator, not a resolver. Answering every query with its own address keeps the sample inside the lab instead of letting it reach the real internet.

7. The tap mirrors all traffic on the lab bridge, so it sees every container's conversation without installing tools on the victim. tcpdump on the victim only sees that host's traffic and requires access to the host.

8. The headers show whether the message legitimately came from the domain it claims. Here SPF failed, DKIM was absent, DMARC failed, and Reply-To used a lookalike domain. The .doc attachment was actually HTML with a JScript block, so the extension concealed the real format and the script was the payload.

9. A DOCX is a ZIP-based OOXML package, and embedded objects are ordinary parts inside that package. A relationship in word/_rels/document.xml.rels points at the object, which in this case is word/embeddings/beacon.js. Macro scanning alone will not find it because the payload is an embedded script, not VBA. Listing the package parts and reading the relationship targets reveals it.

docs.text:
Before you move on to another malware chapter, confirm you can do all of the following without looking them up:
